docs.abstract: The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled Monday that a Border Patrol agent could be sued by the family of a 15-year-old Mexican boy he shot and killed.
docs.snippet: The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled Monday that a Border Patrol agent could be sued by the family of a 15-year-old Mexican boy he shot and killed.
docs.lead_paragraph: The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled Monday that a Border Patrol agent could be sued by the family of a 15-year-old Mexican boy he shot and killed even though the boy was in Mexico at the time of the episode. The agent, Jesus Mesa Jr., shot Sergio Adrian Hernandez Guereca on June 7, 2010, through a barbed wire border fence near El Paso. Mr. Mesa and the Obama administration argued that the agent could not be sued because constitutional protections did not apply since the youth was not in the United States. A three-judge panel of the court, in New Orleans, rejected that argument, saying the agent’s conduct was obviously unlawful, so he did not qualify for immunity.

headline.main: Texas: Panel Rules Agent Can Be Sued Over Shooting Teenager Across Border

(Flix) AMÉLIE (2001) Audrey Tautou, above, in her breakthrough role, plays a French sprite working as a waitress who lays out elaborate practical jokes as payback for those who offend her friends. When she falls in love with Nino (Mathieu Kassovitz), Amélie finds herself incapable of revealing her feelings and instead turns Paris, recreated through sets and computer-generated imagery, into a kind of treasure hunt as she leaves clues about her identity, and he trails after her. docs.abstract: The bungalo where George Orwell was born, in what is now Motihari, India, is being restored.
docs.snippet: The bungalo where George Orwell was born, in what is now Motihari, India, is being restored.
docs.lead_paragraph: The ramshackle three-room bungalow in Motihari, India where George Orwell was born in 1903 is being restored and transformed into a museum that will celebrate the life and career of the essayist and author, The Times of India reported. The renovation, which has been under discussion since 2010, when the house was declared a protected site, is being underwritten by the government of Bihar state, which is hoping the museum will become a tourist attraction. Motihari is in northeastern India, near the border of Nepal. Orwell, who was born Eric Arthur Blair, was born there while his father, Richard Blair, was posted in Bihar as an employee of the Indian Civil Service, to supervise the production of opium for export to China.

headline.main: Orwell Birthplace in India to Become a Museum

docs.lead_paragraph: How do you solve a problem like Melissa McCarthy? That question feels inescapable after watching her try to powerlift “Tammy,” her newest and least funny comedy, all by her lonesome. Ms. McCarthy plays the title bad-luck gal who, shortly after the movie opens, hits a deer and is hit in return, walks away from her broken-down car and into the rest of her tumbledown life. Repeatedly knocked down throughout this knockabout comedy, Tammy takes a licking and keeps on sticking her foot right back in it. She’s a total loser, except in the comedy of misfortune.

docs.abstract: The European Court of Human Rights has upheld a French ban on wearing face-covering veils in public, rejecting arguments that the measure violates religious freedoms.
docs.snippet: The European Court of Human Rights has upheld a French ban on wearing face-covering veils in public, rejecting arguments that the measure violates religious freedoms.
docs.lead_paragraph: The European Court of Human Rights has upheld a French ban on wearing face-covering veils in public, rejecting arguments that the measure violates religious freedoms and bolstering opponents of strict Islamic dress in other parts of Europe. The ban, which took effect three years ago, set French authorities on a collision course with conservative Muslims who said the wearing of such veils by women was an obligation of their faith. Judges at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, said Tuesday that the ban was a legitimate attempt to preserve the norms of France’s diverse society and that it did not infringe on Europe’s Convention on Human Rights. The court was ruling on a case brought by an unidentified Frenchwoman who said the law was discriminatory and violated her freedom of conscience. The 24-year-old woman, a college graduate, requested anonymity for fear of reprisals if her identity became known. France was the first country in Europe to enact such a ban, followed by Belgium.

headline.main: France: European Rights Court Upholds French Ban on Veils

docs.abstract: Julia Leonard’s Either Way L.A. project showcases functional art objects by emerging talent in a space below her Echo Park home.
docs.snippet: Julia Leonard’s Either Way L.A. project showcases functional art objects by emerging talent in a space below her Echo Park home.
docs.lead_paragraph: The unique geography of Los Angeles — both physical and social — tends to encourage the city’s burgeoning art and design communities, especially on the artist-friendly east side, to think outside the white gallery box. Case in point: a rotating monthly pop-up known as Either Way L.A., a 150-square-foot exhibition space nestled in the garden studio beneath the hillside home of Julia Leonard, an artist and curator, in the bohemian enclave (and emerging microscale design hub) of Echo Park. “I wanted to show people in L.A. some things they haven’t seen yet,” she explains, “in an environment that didn’t feel as precious as a four-wall gallery.” Since she began the project a year ago, Leonard has showcased functional objects by exciting young talents from L.A. and beyond, such as the ceramists Jessica Hans and Morgan Peck. Now up is a show by the artist Dane Johnson, “Paintings You Can Wear,” a collection of garments hand-painted with abstract geometric shapes. Leonard devises each show’s theme in collaboration with the artist or designer on view. “Art can be so hard and harsh and it doesn’t need to be,” Leonard says. “I like the idea of running the gallery as if it’s a group effort.”

headline.main: By Design | An L.A. Gallery and Shop So Laid Back, It’s at the Curator’s House

I’ve been looking for a news peg on which to hang some comments on Lilla’s argument, and I think I’ve found one in the news that the ISIS terrorist organization, a.k.a. the de facto government of eastern Syria and western Iraq, has taken the high-risk step of actually declaring a reborn caliphate in its conquered territory. The connection here is that one of Lilla’s themes is the way our ongoing end-of-history era has constricted the Western political imagination, leaving us unable to reckon with the complexities of a wider world where liberal democracy isn’t obviously spreading anymore:

docs.abstract: Ecuador has the right to sue a pair of fugitive bankers in courts in the United States to recover millions of dollars that the men are accused of embezzling, a Florida appellate court has ruled.
docs.snippet: Ecuador has the right to sue a pair of fugitive bankers in courts in the United States to recover millions of dollars that the men are accused of embezzling, a Florida appellate court has ruled.
docs.lead_paragraph: The government of Ecuador has the right to sue a pair of fugitive bankers in courts in the United States to recover millions of dollars that the government accuses the men of having embezzled, a Florida appellate court ruled on Wednesday. The bankers, Roberto and William Isaias, brothers who live in Coral Gables, Fla., have been convicted of embezzling $600 million from Filanbanco, a bank they owned in their native Ecuador. The Ecuadorean government sued them in a Miami court to recover a portion of the $200 million the government claims it is still owed. Last year, a state judge in Miami ruled in favor of the brothers, saying that international law did not allow Ecuador to seize properties in Florida. The Third District Court of Appeal overturned that verdict, ruling that the government was trying to recover funds, not seize property.

headline.main: Government of Ecuador Can Sue Fugitive Bankers in U.S.

docs.abstract: Do donkeys get depressed? Are some aoudads anxious? And what can a zoo’s shrink do to help ease their minds?
docs.snippet: Do donkeys get depressed? Are some aoudads anxious? And what can a zoo’s shrink do to help ease their minds?
docs.lead_paragraph: Dr. Vint Virga likes to arrive at a zoo several hours before it opens, when the sun is still in the trees and the lanes are quiet and the trash cans empty. Many of the animals haven’t yet slipped into their afternoon ma­laise, when they retreat, appearing to wait out the heat and the visitors and not do much of anything. Virga likes to creep to the edge of their enclosures and watch. He chooses a spot and tries not to vary it, he says, “to give the animals a sense of control.” Sometimes he watches an animal for hours, hardly moving. That’s because what to an average zoo visitor looks like frolicking or restlessness or even boredom looks to Virga like a lot more — looks, in fact, like a veritable Russian novel of truculence, joy, sociability, horniness, ire, protectiveness, deference, melancholy and even humor.

docs.abstract: The artist, whose site-specific exhibiton, “Platform: Maya Lin,” opens at the Parrish Museum in Water Mill, N.Y. tomorrow, discusses how her work addresses climate change.
docs.snippet: The artist, whose site-specific exhibiton, “Platform: Maya Lin,” opens at the Parrish Museum in Water Mill, N.Y. tomorrow, discusses how her work addresses climate change.
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1981, Maya Lin first caught the world’s attention with her design for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. Three decades later, she is working on what she calls her “last memorial”: What is Missing?, a nonprofit that blends art and science to raise awareness about the ongoing loss of biodiversity and natural habitats. Man’s precarious relationship to nature is also at the center of Lin’s studio practice, where she uses the tools of a scientist — sonar resonance scans, satellite mapping — to create strikingly minimalist works. Her environmentally-minded site-specific projects, including “Pin River — Sandy,” a ghostly wall-sized installation that maps Hurricane Sandy’s flood plain using straight pins, are the subject of the exhibition “Platform: Maya Lin,” which opens this Friday at the Herzog & De Meuron-designed Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, N.Y. As she readied the show, the artist discussed climate change, art’s power to shift perceptions and the place where the land meets the sea.

headline.main: Q. & A. | Maya Lin on Saving the Planet Through Art

docs.lead_paragraph: The rickshaws of Kolkata, India, remnants of British imperialism, are among the last in the world, but phasing them out has been far from simple. In 2005, Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee called them an “inhuman practice” and pushed for their eradication. But the All Bengal Rickshaw Union protested the ban, claiming that without alternative employment, the drivers would lose their livelihood. The photographer Dougie Wallace, who has a book coming out on taxis in Mumbai, “Road Wallah,” shot the drivers on these pages, many of whom told him they’ve been working for more than 20 years for less than 500 rupees ($8) a day. Still, says Shireen Hyrapiet, an instructor at Oregon State University who has interviewed drivers extensively, many young immigrants see pulling a rickshaw “as a means of upward social mobility.” Marnie Hanel

docs.abstract: Don Carpenter’s posthumous novel follows four aspiring writers during the early, heady days of the Beat scene.
docs.snippet: Don Carpenter’s posthumous novel follows four aspiring writers during the early, heady days of the Beat scene.
docs.lead_paragraph: If Ken Kesey’s “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” prefigured the Age of Aquarius, then Don Carpenter’s semi-­autobiographical “Fridays at Enrico’s” can be read as the swan song of the entire Love Generation. After Carpenter burst onto the West Coast literary scene in 1966, with his gritty first novel, “Hard Rain Falling” (reissued in 2009 by New York Review Books), he became an unofficial adviser to fellow Bay Area writers trying to ride Jack Kerouac’s coattails. Never a hippie celebrity like Richard Brautigan or a living legend like Lawrence Ferlinghetti, Carpenter was a straight man to the more illustrious neo-Beat and -Dada artists of the era. With his moon face, receding hairline, professional discipline and calm demeanor, he was a steadying antidote to the counterculture bedlam of the tumultuous 1960s and beyond.

docs.lead_paragraph: Reviewing a debut novel titled “The Orchard Keeper,” in 1965, the New York Times critic Orville Prescott chastened its author for nearly submerging “his own talents beneath a flood of imitation.” That young author was Cormac McCarthy, and the influence whose weight Prescott saw him sagging beneath belonged to William Faulkner. Among the hand-me-down characteristics Prescott noted: “the wandering pronouns with no visible antecedents; the recondite vocabulary and coined words; the dense prose packed with elaborate figures of speech; the deliberate ambiguity, the hints and withheld information; the confusion in time and place; and the flashbacks that fail to shed much light into the intermittent gloom.” All of these factors, he concluded, made for an exasperating book. “But the wonder,” he pivoted, “is that in spite of them it is also an impressive book.”

docs.snippet: A portrait of the complex, quarrelsome, distinctive artist James McNeill Whistler.
docs.lead_paragraph: Of all the American artists of the 19th century, James Abbott McNeill Whistler was probably the talkiest. In the 1870s, when he painted his famous portrait of his mother, he was living in London, a high-strung expatriate who saw fit to issue mission statements on what seemed like an hourly basis. “Art should be independent of all claptrap,” he declared, believing he had stripped painting of sentimentality and moral uplift and the other trademarks of Victorian culture.

docs.abstract: In an apocalyptic future, a couple seek a stable community as they prepare for the birth of their baby.
docs.snippet: In an apocalyptic future, a couple seek a stable community as they prepare for the birth of their baby.
docs.lead_paragraph: Some dystopian novels, like Cormac ­McCarthy’s “The Road,” explore human relationships in dark, existential post-collapse scenarios, uninterested in either causes or solutions. Others engage with global warming head-on and imagine the possibilities beyond catastrophe, as in Margaret Atwood’s ultimately optimistic Madd­Addam trilogy. But there’s a middle path too — one exemplified by Edan Lepucki’s first novel, “California,” in which characters traverse a cross-section of mid-collapse landscape, framed by the gradual decline of civilization. This approach may seem too optimistic given dire news about melting icecaps and acidic oceans, but it does allow for a reading of the novel as satire, skewering the elements of modern life that have brought us to this tipping point.

docs.snippet: In Tom Bouman’s “Dry Bones in the Valley,” an elderly recluse finds a stranger dead on his property in northeastern Pennsylvania.
docs.lead_paragraph: Some stories are so sad, you want them to have the comfort of a gentle storytelling voice. Tom Bouman extends that kindness in DRY BONES IN THE VALLEY (Norton, $24.95), his beautifully written first novel set in the mountainous region of northeastern Pennsylvania that sits atop the Marcellus Shale, a vast geological treasure, prized and exploited for its natural gas resources. With neighbors feuding over whether to lease drilling rights to companies accused of poisoning the environment, it’s no wonder that a crazy old recluse like Aubrey Dunigan would be testy with anyone he finds hanging around his decrepit farm. But these hills are also overrun with meth cookers, dope dealers and Mexican drug cartels. So just because a stranger is found dead on his property doesn’t make poor old Aubrey a murderer.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Where else in the world does one have the freedom to contradict oneself?” Ilan Stavans asks in “A Most Imperfect Union,” a witty alternative history of the United States from the arrival of European settlers to the shooting of Trayvon Martin and the Mars rover landing in 2012. It’s a prequel to “Latino USA” — his previous collaboration with the illustrator Lalo Alcaraz, a cartoon history of Latino culture in America — and even more ambitious. This time the focus is on “the dispossessed and minority groups of all stripes, as well as individuals known and unknown to most students of American history.” What the books have in common, Stavans writes, is “sarcasm.”

docs.abstract: A group of Latino immigrants faces the challenges of assimilation in Cristina Henríquez’s novel.
docs.snippet: A group of Latino immigrants faces the challenges of assimilation in Cristina Henríquez’s novel.
docs.lead_paragraph: If it’s true that — in the long tradition of “Don Quixote” — all novels are about road trips, then perhaps no novels detail the challenges of the journey more than immigrants’ tales. The tradition is long and worldwide. The hearts of the downtrodden, the forgotten and neglected, swell with hope at the prospect of starting over somewhere. They collect their courage along with essential belongings and begin the trek to the unforeseen. No matter if the stories they’ve heard about the new country are exaggerated and acculturation is a frightening hurdle, it will — it must — be better than the present situation. In this spirit, the characters in ­Cristina Henríquez’s new novel, “The Book of Unknown Americans,” have come to the United States.

docs.snippet: Jordan Ellenberg, whose “How Not to Be Wrong” is No. 15 on the hardcover nonfiction list, recently said about math: “We know nothing. Right now we are standing in a tiny circle of light around our feet.”
docs.lead_paragraph: By the Numbers: Jordan Ellenberg’s math-based guide to life, “How Not to Be Wrong,” is at No. 15 in its second week on the hardcover nonfiction list. Ellenberg is a star mathematician at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, where the local alternative weekly recently asked him about his specialty in number theory — “addition and subtraction and multiplication, all the things you can do with numbers,” as Ellenberg put it. “Haven’t we already figured all that stuff out?” the reporter wondered, and Ellenberg laughed. “We know nothing,” he said. “Right now we are standing in a tiny circle of light around our feet, and every 1,000 years, we push that circle out just a little bit. Every time someone sticks his toe out beyond that circle, it opens up whole worlds of inquiry.” Ellenberg is also a published novelist (I met him at a summer fiction workshop almost 20 years ago), but he told the Madison weekly that one of the things he’d learned in his creative writing classes was how much he liked math.

docs.lead_paragraph: As the World Cup moves into the quarterfinal, semifinal, and final rounds, one Paris establishment is offering the ultimate setting for watching a match: Le Royal Monceau Raffles Paris, the grand Philippe Starck-redesigned hotel situated in the Eighth Arondissement. The hotel’s private theater, with seating for 99, will screen the playoff matches in live broadcast, enhanced with a few choice amenities. There will be strawberry and basil caipirinhas (in deference to the host country) and a pop-up Veuve Clicquot Champagne terrace (it’s still France, after all). There will be caramelized popcorn, made by the pastry chef and macaron maestro Pierre Hermé, to snack on, and a three-course dinner option from the hotel’s Michelin-starred restaurant, La Cuisine. And there will be state-of-the-art televisions specially installed by Sony for the occasion. While the setting is opulent (and the dress code specifies “no board shorts or flip-flops”), the mood will be spirited, according to the hotel’s manager, Pierre-Alexandre Francin. “Guests love the fact that they’re allowed to let loose, scream and shout whenever someone scores a goal,” he says.

headline.main: In Paris, the Ultimate Place to Watch a World Cup Match

docs.snippet: A pavilion resembling a space module, designed by the Chilean architect Smiljan Radic, has opened on the lawn of the Serpentine Gallery in London.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — For the 15th year, the Serpentine Gallery has commissioned an architect to design a temporary structure on its front lawn in Kensington Gardens here. Generally, those who are chosen have not built anything in Britain before. Over the years, Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid, Jean Nouvel, Sou Fujimoto and Rem Koolhaas have each planted a pavilion here, some more bizarre than others. This year’s creation, by the Chilean architect Smiljan Radic, is a kind of alien space pod resting on 62 tons of giant quarry stones. Fashioned from semi-translucent, glass-reinforced plastic, like the Fiberglas used to build yachts, it arrived in 66 pieces and took six weeks to install. Inside are a cafe and space for events that bring together art, poetry, literature and film by emerging creators.

headline.main: Space Pod Alights at the Serpentine Gallery

docs.lead_paragraph: Anchored by a magical early work by Joan Jonas, this small group show, organized by the painter Mary Simpson, runs wild with the theme of multiplied and divided selves. It should be seen especially for Ms. Jonas’s “Glass Puzzle,” a video installation from the early 1970s that involves two female performers, two cameras and various ways of distancing the spectator from the action. (Ms. Jonas, who once called the piece a “puzzle in space,” fed a live performance to a television monitor and then aimed a camera at the monitor, so that we ultimately see a fuzzy view of the women that’s further marred by reflections on the screen.)

docs.abstract: Do you prefer nature or culture? Indulging in local food or burning it off? Choose your own combination during a weekend in western Massachusetts.
docs.snippet: Do you prefer nature or culture? Indulging in local food or burning it off? Choose your own combination during a weekend in western Massachusetts.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Berkshires, I used to think, were nothing special. Only after I left my childhood home in western Massachusetts did I learn that not every American countryside is crisscrossed by so many lines of music and literature, by crumbling stone walls running like half-forgotten stories through farms and woodlands, by ellipses of deep green hills fading to blue. The Berkshires, of course, have been beloved for centuries. Long before their Gilded Age heyday as the “Inland Newport,” a guillotine-fleeing lady-in-waiting of Marie Antoinette remarked on the region’s fertility and “majestic forests.” A sense of that history is one reason that I keep returning to favorite Berkshire spots. But this summer new attractions and renovations are making their mark on the county’s cultural, natural and culinary landscapes, and the decisions you’ll face every Berkshire morning — old or new? art or the outdoors? — are getting harder than ever to make.

headline.main: 36 Hours in the Berkshires

docs.lead_paragraph: How about ... an Alleyscapes? The Shubert and Booth theaters, built in 1913 west of Broadway on 44th and 45th Streets, created one of the most unusual thoroughfares in New York, the through-block passage known as Shubert Alley. Although an incidental feature at first, it is now one of the most important gathering spaces in the theater district. Maryann Chach, director of the Shubert Archive, has given the odd space its first full treatment in the current issue of the archive’s newsletter, "The Passing Show," but there are still some unanswered questions.

docs.abstract: Diplomats have resolved an unusually bitter dispute over how much United Nations peacekeepers should be paid.
docs.snippet: Diplomats have resolved an unusually bitter dispute over how much United Nations peacekeepers should be paid.
docs.lead_paragraph: Diplomats on Thursday resolved an unusually bitter dispute over how much United Nations peacekeepers should be paid. The countries that send troops, mostly from South Asia and Africa, are currently paid an average of $1,210 per soldier per month, a rate that has not changed for about a decade. The payments will increase gradually over the next four years, according to an agreement that is expected to be approved by the United Nations General Assembly, to just over $1,400. The countries contributing troops had wanted a rate of more than $1,700, based on an estimate provided by the United Nations Secretariat. Countries that fund peacekeeping missions — the United States, Japan and France are the largest funders — called that demand unrealistic. The total peacekeeping budget has increased to $8.6 billion, a record, though as the United Nations points out, that is less than 1 percent of total military expenditures worldwide. Each country decides how much of the reimbursement rate goes to individual soldiers.

headline.main: U.N. Peacekeepers’ Pay Dispute Is Resolved

The protests in the capital, Cairo, were scattered and in some neighborhoods, small and quickly dispersed by riot police officers. At least one protester was killed. Mr. Morsi’s supporters have held regular rallies since his ouster on July 3, 2013, but the protests have dwindled in the face of an increasingly harsh government crackdown against Islamists and other dissidents that has included mass killings by the security forces, the arrests of tens of thousands of people and a ban on demonstrations. Separately on Thursday, an explosion in a Cairo apartment killed two people who the authorities said were militants in the process of preparing a bomb.

They have been smart, so far, to carefully maintain individual careers. Their latest husband-wife project, though, is an appealing recording: a program of diverse “Love Duets.” Ms. Pérez’s warm, penetrating voice matches well but also contrasts interestingly with Mr. Costello’s rich, virile sound. They excel in duets from Massenet’s “Manon,” Verdi’s “La Traviata,” Gounod’s “Faust” and, best of all, the tender “Cherry Duet” from Mascagni’s “L’amico Fritz.” “One Hand, One Heart” from Bernstein’s “West Side Story” is disappointing: too somber, slow and self-consciously operatic. docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: German Mercedes drivers win the automobile Grand Prix in France in 1914.
docs.lead_paragraph: The greatest automobile race of the year, the Grand Prix, organized by the Automobile Club de France, ended yesterday on the Lyons circuit in a definite and conclusive German victory. Lautenschlager, driving a Mercedes machine, finished first; Wagner, also driving a Mercedes, was second, and Salzer, another German, in the same make of machine, was third. Never since 1895, when the Automobile Club de France organized its first big competition, the race from Paris to Bordeaux, has an automobile race attracted so huge a crowd. Even the Paris-Vienna and Paris-Madrid contests of 1902 and 1903 were eclipsed. Lyons was hardly recognizable. It was the magnet for hundreds of automobiles and thousands and thousands of spectators. On Friday many of the cafés remained open all night. The streets were lined with automobiles unable to obtain garage, and the pavements were black with a multitude of pedestrians moving, because they could not help it, at a snail’s pace. — The New York Herald, European Edition, July 5, 1914

headline.main: 1914: Mercedes Finishes First in Grand Prix

docs.lead_paragraph: BERLIN — Germany is faced with seemingly insurmountable obstacles to real preparedness for war, according to the semi-annual economic review of the Reichskredit Gesellschaft, which was published here today. Just at a time when the entire world is studying the Reich’s economic position in an effort to determine its war potential, this mid- year report reveals there are still a number of monkey wrenches in the country’s war machinery. Germany apparently is still handicapped by a severe shortage of labor, food products and raw materials. The economic expert, who summarized the report, found that the labor shortage is one of the weakest spots in Germany’s militarized economy. Even with the present size of fine armed forces, there is a shortage of one million workers and the only apparent way to increase the number of industrial and building workers is to import more foreign labor and ‘‘comb out superfluous labor’’ in the retail trades. It is estimated that the country could get 450,000 laborers by the combing-out process. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 5, 1939.

headline.main: 1939: Nazi Germany Unprepared for World War II

docs.abstract: Encourage people to do something for its own sake, not for its benefits.
docs.snippet: Encourage people to do something for its own sake, not for its benefits.
docs.lead_paragraph: THERE are two kinds of motive for engaging in any activity: internal and instrumental. If a scientist conducts research because she wants to discover important facts about the world, that’s an internal motive, since discovering facts is inherently related to the activity of research. If she conducts research because she wants to achieve scholarly renown, that’s an instrumental motive, since the relation between fame and research is not so inherent. Often, people have both internal and instrumental motives for doing what they do.

docs.abstract: Harlow East is the quintessential Hamptons restaurant, with expansive water views and a blue and white décor delivered with nautical flair. It’s the Sag Harbor outpost of the Manhattan restaurant Harlow, on East 56th Street.
docs.snippet: Harlow East is the quintessential Hamptons restaurant, with expansive water views and a blue and white décor delivered with nautical flair. It’s the Sag Harbor outpost of the Manhattan restaurant Harlow, on East 56th Street.
docs.lead_paragraph: Wide, white and airy, with shiny wood floors and a blue and white décor delivered with nautical flair, Harlow East is the quintessential Hamptons restaurant, offering expansive views of the water both inside and out. The restaurant, which opened on Memorial Day weekend, is the Sag Harbor outpost of the Manhattan restaurant Harlow, on East 56th Street. Neither place has anything to do with the Depression-era actress Jean Harlow, but both are named after the 8-year-old daughter of Richie Notar, the owner. Harlow East is located on Long Wharf in the former home of another New York City success story: B. Smith. If you go, try to snag a table on the wide porch under the crisp, navy blue awning to take in the best bay views. After all, you’ll be paying for it.

docs.lead_paragraph: IT’S July, and it’s starting to get hot. This month last year — on Friday, July 19, 2013 — New York City broke its electricity usage record. And as more heat rolled in, the blackouts did too, in Washington, Baltimore, Philadelphia and Boston — no major metropolitan area on the East Coast was spared. Our only connection was that we had all recently given birth at Stanford Hospital in Palo Alto, Calif., and, as recommended by our doctors, had signed up for the New Mother training class. docs.abstract: And Svensson vindicated.
docs.snippet: And Svensson vindicated.
docs.lead_paragraph: OK, this is fairly amazing. I’ve written often about sadomonetarism among central bankers — the evident urge to find some reason, any reason, to raise interest rates despite high unemployment and low inflation. The most influential hive of this kind of thinking is the Bank for International Settlements, which for some reason commands great respect even though it offers an ever-changing rationale — inflation! Any day now! Or maybe not! Financial stability! — for its never-changing advocacy of tight money. But the place where policy makers most dramatically gave in to this urge is Sweden, where the majority at the Riksbank decided to indulge its rate-hike vice while freezing out one of the world’s leading experts on deflation risks, my friend and former colleague Lars Svensson.

headline.main: Swedish Sadomonetarist Setback

docs.abstract: We fail to appreciate how radically contingent our lives really are.
docs.snippet: We fail to appreciate how radically contingent our lives really are.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s a disturbing thought: All of us are alive today thanks at least partly to some mass atrocity that was committed in the past. This is because war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and ethnic cleansing invariably affect who is born after them. Who knows how many of us can claim, “Even if the Holocaust had not occurred, I would still have been born”? And if you can, perhaps because you were conceived before 1933 or shortly afterward without having been influenced in some way by the effects of Hitlerism, what about the Crusades or slavery in America? Anyone who reflects on the unjust death of others will be surprised at how much his or her own right to be is put in question, to the point where his or her place on this earth can appear as a usurpation. This might not be obvious at first so let’s slow down a bit.

docs.abstract: Readers comment on my column about an innocent man who spent 25 years in prison for murder
docs.snippet: Readers comment on my column about an innocent man who spent 25 years in prison for murder
docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column looks at the flaws in our criminal justice system through the remarkable story of Michael Morton, author of a new memoir. Morton was a middle class guy in Austin with no criminal record, and he came home from work one day to find his wife murdered–and himself a key suspect. He spent the next 25 years in prison for murdering her, partly because the authorities suppressed exculpatory evidence. It’s as harrowing a story as you can imagine, and it’s a good starting point for a discussion about what to do to improve the justice system. Three elements of an improvement would be, I think: 1.) an end to the disastrous mass incarceration experiment that began in the 1970’s; 2.) an improved network of mental health services, so that prisons and jails are no longer our default mental health system; 3.) improved treatment programs for addicts, so that a failed war on drugs no longer fills up prisons and jails. That’s all a bit glib, I realize, and there’s no silver bullet solution the problems of drugs, but it’s impossible to read Morton’s memoir without feeling that the present system is an appalling and expensive mess.

headline.main: When “Justice” Isn’t Just

docs.abstract: Before Allen Ginsberg and the Beats descended on San Francisco, there was James Broughton.
docs.snippet: Before Allen Ginsberg and the Beats descended on San Francisco, there was James Broughton.
docs.lead_paragraph: Before Allen Ginsberg and the Beats descended on San Francisco, there was James Broughton (1913-99), a poet, experimental filmmaker, pansexual free spirit and proto-hippie who, like Ginsberg, was a spiritual descendant of Walt Whitman. His exuberant life and times are recalled in “Big Joy: The Adventures of James Broughton,” now available on DVD and on demand. Directed by Stephen Silha, Eric Slade and Dawn Logsdon, the documentary captures the euphoric mood of bohemian San Francisco just after World War II and includes many excerpts from his exhortatory poetry. For much of his life, he followed the dictum of his motto, “Follow your weird.”

headline.main: Imbibing the Joys of a Lusty Poet

docs.abstract: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: Mexican rebels sponsored by money from the United States in 1914.
docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: Mexican rebels sponsored by money from the United States in 1914.
docs.lead_paragraph: EL PASO, Tex. — More than a million dollars of gold from big business sources in the eastern States alone have been poured into the Mexican rebel coffers during the last nine months. This is admitted by Constitutionalists of prominence. It is added that since the split between Generals Carranza and Villa much money has been withheld, and the rebel cause now faces serious embarrassment. The bitterness engendered by the clash of the two leaders has loosened tongues, and the facts are now known for the first time. The money has come here in single drafts for $50,000 at a time on two local banks transferring the funds. It is impossible to get documental proof, but it is believed that most of it has gone to the honest needs of warfare. So acute has become the need of more money that Senor Alberto Madero has hurried to New York to impress the capitalists alleged to be financing the revolution with the necessity of funds. General Villa is trying to raise money by concessions for the sale of dynamite and the exportation of cattle. The Pearson and Guggenheim lumbering and mining interests have been allowed to reopen. Unusual protection is being afforded the latter. — The New York Herald, European Edition, July 7, 1914

docs.abstract: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: A crowd of fans greeted the Beatles at the premiere of their first film, in 1964.
docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: A crowd of fans greeted the Beatles at the premiere of their first film, in 1964.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — Twelve thousand screaming teen-agers packed Piccadilly Circus tonight [July 6] for a look at the Beatles as they attended the world première of their first film, ‘‘A Hard Day’s Night.’’ Also present for the charity première were Princess Margaret and her husband, Lord Snowdon, but they received a much smaller ovation from the crowd. The Beatles — Paul McCartney, George Harrison, John Lennon and Ringo Starr — were presented to the royal couple in the lobby of the theater. ‘‘What do you think of the film?’’ asked the princess. ‘‘I don’t think we are very good, ma’am,’’ Mr. McCartney said with a smile. ‘‘But the director is very good.’’ As soon as the royal party left, usherettes in dresses printed with the Beatles’ faces rushed up to the quartet and asked them to sign their dresses. Ambulance men carried off about 20 fainting girls including one who screamed from her stretcher: ‘‘Let me up! I want to see them!’’ — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 7, 1964.

headline.main: 1964: Fans Scream for Beatles at Movie Premiere

docs.abstract: The director of two documentaries about human rights abuses in Guatemala said that she planned to correct inaccuracies in those films, The Associated Press reported.
docs.snippet: The director of two documentaries about human rights abuses in Guatemala said that she planned to correct inaccuracies in those films, The Associated Press reported.
docs.lead_paragraph: The director of two documentaries about human rights abuses in Guatemala said that she planned to correct inaccuracies in those films, including blaming the country’s military for a village massacre, The Associated Press reported. The director, Pamela Yates, said in a statement that the decision resulted from investigations into the circumstances surrounding the killing of 17 villagers recounted in her 1984 film, “When the Mountains Tremble.” The scene took place in Batzul, where a local woman told the filmmakers that the men responsible for the murders wore military uniforms. Later reports and a recent visit by Ms. Yates revealed that the men had been members of guerrilla forces dressed as army soldiers. Ms. Yates said that she intended “to make a correction that will clarify what happened in this scene” in both that film and her 2011 documentary, “Granito: How to Nail a Dictator.” “When the Mountains Tremble” won multiple honors upon its release, including the Special Jury Award at the Sundance Film Festival.

headline.main: Director to Correct Films on Guatemala
headline.print_headline: Director to Correct Films on Guatemala

docs.abstract: The radio shock jock Anthony Cumia has scratched off another of his nine lives.
docs.snippet: The radio shock jock Anthony Cumia has scratched off another of his nine lives.
docs.lead_paragraph: The radio shock jock Anthony Cumia has scratched off another of his nine lives: He was fired last week from SiriusXM’s “Opie & Anthony” radio show. The decision came after Mr. Cumia, below, posted what the company described in a news release as “racially charged and hate-filled remarks” on his personal Twitter account over a run-in with a black woman in Times Square. The tweets, as well as expletive-laced reactions toward his firing, have been removed from his account but can be found online. In the news release, Patrick Reilly, a SiriusXM spokesman, called Mr. Cumia’s comments “abhorrent” and “wholly inconsistent” with the company’s values. Fans have taken to social media to express support of Mr. Cumia, some saying they’ve canceled their SiriusXM subscriptions. An online petition to reinstate him had reached nearly 7,000 signatures through early Sunday afternoon. The show’s other host, Greg Hughes, a.k.a. Opie, posted on Twitter that he was devastated and would meet with SiriusXM on Tuesday. The hosts have a history of trouble. In 1998, Mr. Cumia and Mr. Hughes were fired from a Boston radio station for an April Fools’ prank in which they extensively, and falsely, reported that the city’s mayor had died in a traffic accident. In 2002, their syndicated show in New York was canceled after they broadcast a live account of a couple supposedly having sex in St. Patrick’s Cathedral. And in 2007, their XM Radio show was suspended for 30 days because of a bit about violent sex and Condoleezza Rice.

headline.main: No More Anthony on ‘Opie & Anthony’
headline.print_headline: No More Anthony on ‘Opie & Anthony’

(HBO) DANGEROUS ACTS STARRING THE UNSTABLE ELEMENTS OF BELARUS (2014) Since 2005, the Belarus Free Theater, including Yana Rusakevich, above, has addressed social and political issues in performances in and around Minsk, the country’s capital and the troupe’s base, often infuriating the government of President Aleksandr Lukashenko but rallying international supporters like Tom Stoppard and Jude Law. This documentary, directed by Madeleine Sackler, presents some of those works, including “Being Harold Pinter,” in which actors struggle to break free of a plastic sheet, and “Minsk 2011,” which pantomimes a police crackdown on a peaceful protest. “The scenes of protest and police brutality include footage gleaned from hundreds of hours filmed in collaboration with a cinematographer in Belarus (whom Ms. Sackler directed over Skype) and then smuggled out of the country,” Stephen Holden wrote in The New York Times. “The Belarus Free Theater, whose members are as articulate as they are talented, continue to spread the message of determined resistance to oppression.”

docs.abstract: Why Lincoln used the controversial pocket veto to kill the Wade-Davis bill.
docs.snippet: Why Lincoln used the controversial pocket veto to kill the Wade-Davis bill.
docs.lead_paragraph: On the morning of July 4, 1864, as Congress was preparing to adjourn for the summer, Abraham Lincoln was busy in an office at the Capitol signing bills. Senator Charles Sumner hovered nearby “in a state of intense anxiety.” George Boutwell, a representative from Massachusetts, paced nervously. Senator Zachariah Chandler of Michigan kept asking anyone who would listen if one particular bill had been signed. Told no, he spoke with Lincoln who, according to the president’s secretary John Hay, said, “this bill was placed before me a few minutes before Congress adjourns. It is a matter of too much importance to be swallowed in that way.”

headline.main: The Battle Over Reconstruction

docs.snippet: A winning combination: sweet, juicy watermelon paired with salty cheese and pungent onions.
docs.lead_paragraph: I love watermelon and feta salad, whether the watermelon is grilled or not. The sweet, juicy watermelon against the salty, creamy feta and pungent onions is a winning combination. This version introduces heat and char. Throw the watermelon slices, with the rind, onto the grill after or before you’ve grilled your meat or fish or vegetables. Grill them on both sides until just charred, then cut away the rinds and dice up the melon for the salad.

docs.lead_paragraph: It goes without saying that if the renowned, elusive music producer and Def Jam Records co-founder Rick Rubin gets excited about someone, they’re probably destined for great things. Now the man who turned the Beastie Boys and the Red Hot Chili Peppers into icons has tapped the Australian folk-blues sibling duo Angus and Julia Stone as his new protégés. “It’s few and far between that I hear something that really excites me,” says Rubin, who’s notorious for rarely speaking to the press. “I heard their music and it really moved me. They make the kind of songs that I can listen to over and over again for a long period of time. They have hypnotic, poetic depth.” What Rubin didn’t know when he contacted the pair — who started making music together in 2006 — was that not only did they have no plans to write any further songs at the time, but they flat-out weren’t getting along at all. “It was only when I reached out to them that they decided to get together to make the album we eventually made, and through that process had a family healing and are better friends today than they, I think, have ever been,” Rubin says. “None of this was intentional. It just happened, and it’s a pretty beautiful part of the story.”

headline.main: A Video Debut from Rick Rubin’s New Protégés, Angus and Julia Stone
headline.print_headline: Sibling Revelry

docs.abstract: The strikingly graphic correspondence from Harding, perhaps the worst chief executive in U.S. history, to his longtime mistress.
docs.snippet: The strikingly graphic correspondence from Harding, perhaps the worst chief executive in U.S. history, to his longtime mistress.
docs.lead_paragraph: Warren Harding is not the most beloved of American presidents. Two of the earliest polls to assess presidential popularity, conducted in 1948 and 1962, ranked him last and last among chief executives. Harding served only briefly, from 1921 to 1923, before he died in office, but his administration has been widely regarded as visionless, ineffectual and corrupt. He slashed immigration quotas, appointed his cronies — one of whom, his secretary of the interior, accepted bribes from oil companies in what became known as the Teapot Dome scandal — and brought an end to the famously reform-minded eras of Teddy Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson. Perhaps the best that can be said about Harding is that he seems to have been conscious of his defects. “I am not fit for this office and should never have been here,” he once conceded.

headline.main: The Letters That Warren G. Harding’s Family Didn’t Want You to See
headline.print_headline: All the President's Pen

docs.lead_paragraph: Big, shiny Chelsea galleries are not the only ones that can present missing chunks of recent art history. Canada, working with the Paris-based Galerie Bernard Ceysson, is staging the first American survey of some painters of the relatively unknown French Supports/Surfaces art movement, which was active in the late 1960s, ’70s and early ’80s. With so much of current abstraction in back-to-basics mode, the show is timely, revealing the strengths and pitfalls of its artists’ approach. Some of this stuff looks alive and pertinent; some of it looks ordinary and inert.

docs.abstract: Emily Mae Smith’s Pop-style paintings at Junior Projects comment on sex and gender with satirical ingenuity.
docs.snippet: Emily Mae Smith’s Pop-style paintings at Junior Projects comment on sex and gender with satirical ingenuity.
docs.lead_paragraph: Bucking the messy abstraction trend, Emily Mae Smith’s Pop-style paintings comment on sex and gender with satirical ingenuity. Two posterlike works on view in this pint-size gallery mimic the cover of The Studio, a late-Victorian art magazine, with the title lettered at the top and the Art Nouveau-style image of a female artist painting in her studio rendered in thin black lines on white grounds. To each of these genteel images, Ms. Smith has added the realistic, semi-transparent color image of a much-enlarged piece of fruit — a banana and a tomato — highlighting the idea of the woman as a desirable commodity.

headline.main: Emily Mae Smith: ‘Novelty Court’

docs.lead_paragraph: Sia goes over the top almost immediately on her new album, “1000 Forms of Fear.” When the chorus of “Chandelier” arrives, a simulated orchestra crashes in, and her voice appears in a strenuous high register, belting, “I’m gonna swing from the chandelier, ” with an I-dare-myself upward leap on the last syllable of “chandelier.” Still aloft, she repeats “from the chandelier” and leaps even higher. docs.lead_paragraph: As editors piled in for the Christian Dior fall 2014 couture presentation today, taking in the classic white orchids that lined the walls around the futuristic runway space (shaped a bit like a round U.F.O.), the collection’s theme — a connection between old and new, past and present — began to make itself apparent. The show began, and the house’s artistic director Raf Simons launched his audience into a sort of time travel with his range of references. He embellished archetypal silhouettes like loose, flapperesque dresses; wide-through-the-hips, Marie Antoinette-style gowns; and baggy, one-piece flight suits with anachronistic details like sophisticated embroidery and fresh prints. Among the many knockout looks in the show, it was hard to ignore the ornate justacorps jacket with a matching gilet underneath. Finished off with a simple black top and trousers, it made for a truly modern ensemble that ushered the couture era right into the now.

headline.main: At Dior, Historical References Translated to Modern Style

docs.lead_paragraph: Venezuelan authorities on Monday welcomed home a painting by the artist Henri Matisse more than a decade after it had disappeared from a Caracas museum. The painting, “Odalisque in Red Pants,” was recovered in 2012 by F.B.I. agents in Miami when they arrested two people and charged them with trying to sell the long-missing artwork. Officials do not know when it was stolen from the Contemporary Art Museum of Caracas, where it was part of the museum’s collection, because the thieves put up a fake version of the painting in its place — a ruse that was discovered in 2002. Photographs showed that the fake, which experts said was crudely executed, was in place at least as early as 2000. News of the painting’s recovery two years ago caused a stir in Venezuela, and officials on Monday made a show of bringing it home, with a live television broadcast from the Caracas airport. When it was recovered, American officials said the painting was worth $3 million.

headline.main: Venezuela: Stolen Matisse Painting Returned
headline.print_headline: Venezuela: Stolen Art Returns

docs.lead_paragraph: India’s Supreme Court ruled Monday that Shariah courts, which are run by the dictates of Islamic law, had no legal status and were not legally binding. In the court’s judgment, fatwas, or orders declared by Muslim clerics, were deemed to have “no legal status” though they were not found to be illegal, and individuals may follow the Shariah rulings if they wish. The court said, however, that a religious leader “has no authority or powers to impose his opinion and enforce his fatwa on anyone,” adding that legally sanctioned fatwas have “no place in independent India under our constitutional scheme.”

docs.abstract: The marriages of gay men and lesbians who work for the United Nations Secretariat will be recognized by the organization if they have been wed in a jurisdiction where same-sex unions are legal.
docs.snippet: The marriages of gay men and lesbians who work for the United Nations Secretariat will be recognized by the organization if they have been wed in a jurisdiction where same-sex unions are legal.
docs.lead_paragraph: The marriages of gay men and lesbians who work for the United Nations Secretariat will be recognized by the organization if they have been wed in a jurisdiction where same-sex unions are legal, including New York. Previously, the secretariat, the body of employees who work under the secretary general, deferred to the laws of a staff member’s home country in classifying his or her marital status: Same-sex unions were recognized by the United Nations only if the employee’s home country deemed such marriages to be legal. The change, said the organization’s deputy spokesman, Farhan Haq, reflects Secretary General Ban Ki-moon’s support for “greater equality for all staff.” The new rule was announced in an internal staff bulletin, Mr. Haq said Monday. It expands the civil rights of gay and lesbian employees, even as many of the United Nations’ member states, including Uganda, whose foreign minister assumes the presidency of the United Nations General Assembly in September, crack down on their own gay and lesbian citizens.

headline.main: A Victory for Same-Sex Unions

docs.abstract: Nearly one billion people worldwide defecate in the open, the United Nations said in a report released Monday, which calls for greater effort and funding to redress inadequate sanitation.
docs.snippet: Nearly one billion people worldwide defecate in the open, the United Nations said in a report released Monday, which calls for greater effort and funding to redress inadequate sanitation.
docs.lead_paragraph: Nearly one billion people worldwide defecate in the open, and such bad sanitation practices can endanger the health of children who live and play nearby, the United Nations said in a report released Monday. The report, which calls for greater effort and funding to redress inadequate sanitation, measures the world’s progress on the so-called Millennium Development Goals intended to improve the health and well-being of the global poor. The report notes some advances: A greater number of children are living past their fifth birthday. As many girls as boys are enrolled in primary school. Extreme poverty has been halved since 1990. But about one in five people in the developing world still lives on less than $1.25 a day; about 25 percent of the world’s children suffer from stunted growth, reflecting the effects of chronic hunger; and nearly half of all pregnant women did not see a doctor during their pregnancy.

headline.main: U.N. Report Calls for Public Sanitation Funding
headline.print_headline: Report on Development Goals

docs.lead_paragraph: My colleague Bruce Feiler and I are arguing a new question on Room for Debate today: To Camp, or Not to Camp? His 9-year-old daughters left last week for what he hopes will be their first summer of sleep-away camp; they’ll be gone for seven weeks. My children are home and largely (although far from totally) unscheduled. Apart from some assorted day camps, they’re spending the summer wandering around the house, complaining that “there’s nothing to do” until they disappear and discover that there actually is. Bruce and I found that our family differences might have their roots in tradition (I never went to camp, he did), but that we also saw summer freedom very differently. His fall/winter 2014 couture presentation held today didn’t compete with that infamous show, but instead fell on the other end of the eye-candy spectrum, offering a look that was restrained yet undeniably chic. The collection’s pared-back sensibility was inspired by a now-defunct 1930s Le Corbusier apartment on the Champs Élysées. Like that apartment’s mash-up of design motifs — a gold baroque mirror that sat atop a modern outdoor fireplace, for example — Lagerfeld’s designs married the old and new. Case in point: this modern-silhouetted maxi dress with ornate gold embroidery. Paired with a coordinating messenger bag, it made for a standout look that lent fresh new meaning to the term “matchy-matchy.”

docs.lead_paragraph: If Jake Hoffman looks familiar, it’s not just because of his striking resemblance to a certain icon of the silver screen with whom he shares a surname. The 33-year-old — who, yes, happens to be the son of Dustin Hoffman — has been acting since the age of 7, when he appeared in his father’s classic film “Rain Man” (he was an extra eating pancakes in a diner). Since then, he has been cast in “I Heart Huckabees,” “Arrested Development” and “The Wolf of Wall Street” (in which he had a small but memorable role as the shoe designer Steve Madden) and he even played his own father’s grandson in HBO’s ill-fated series “Luck.” Since graduating from NYU’s film school in 2003, Hoffman has tried his hand at writing and directing, and completed a trio of short films. Now, with the release of his debut full-length feature, “Asthma” — which he wrote, produced and directed, and which premiered today at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic — Hoffman is staking out a film career on his own terms.

headline.main: Jake Hoffman (Yes, He’s the Son of Dustin) Makes His Debut as a Director

docs.lead_paragraph: Couture looks are by definition designed to make a grand entrance. But this week, a handful of houses showed frothy, lavishly tiered ball gowns that proved especially eye-catching in the mix. The first of these cloudlike confections popped up last night during the Giambattista Valli finale, which consisted of a small series of ombré gowns (and evening skirts, which were paired simply with poplin shirts). Then this morning at Chanel, Karl Lagerfeld interrupted his parade of white dresses with a soft, billowing light-blue dress complete with equally full feather sleeves. And finally, at this evening’s Armani Privé show, one of the many red dress options from the designer included a voluminous strapless number topped with an equally dramatic veil.

docs.lead_paragraph: Earlier this year, I wrote a column on a crucial sociological distinction between religious affiliation and religious practice in American life — specifically, the way that the strong association between social capital and religious faith only really obtains for people who are active in their faith, and the way that a great deal of social ruin in our nation is concentrated in communities (mostly working class) where religion has half-retreated, leaving a kind of identitarian, Christian-ish residue that either has no real effect on people’s choices or (possibly) shapes them for the worse.

Absolutely when it’s this one, taken from live performances in 2013 that Michael Tilson Thomas conducted with the San Francisco Symphony at the orchestra’s home hall. The cast, led by Alexandra Silber as Maria and Cheyenne Jackson as Tony, who bring youthful ardor, beguiling voices and dramatic immediacy to their roles, is ideal. This is a nearly complete version of Bernstein’s score, with lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. The symphonic richness of the playing is an asset. docs.lead_paragraph: Just south of the hip Palermo Soho neighborhood, a staunchly working-class Buenos Aires barrio is undergoing a quiet metamorphosis. Long home to the city’s Jewish community, Villa Crespo’s streets are lined with mom-and-pop shops, onetime factories and faded colonial facades that have mostly remained outside the trendsetters’ purview. But given its prime location — enterprising real estate agents are trying to rechristen the enclave Palermo Queens, much to the chagrin of longtime residents — an influx of hip restaurants and boutiques was inevitable. At the moment, the neighborhood still feels removed from the city’s hubbub, but more locals are descending upon its cobbled lanes.

docs.abstract: The case of Deeb Salem, a former Goldman Sachs trader, highlights an arbitration system that is weighted toward the big Wall Street firms, William D. Cohan writes in the Street Scene column.

docs.lead_paragraph: Deeb Salem, the former Goldman Sachs trader who helped devise the firm’s brilliant and highly profitable proprietary bet against the mortgage market, has never been shy about trumpeting his accomplishments. Mr. Salem no longer works at Goldman — he decamped to GoldenTree Asset Management, a New York hedge fund, in 2012 — but his continuing lawsuit, which contends the firm shortchanged him about $21 million in bonus and deferred compensation during the years after the financial crisis, raises fresh questions about the fairness of Wall Street’s compensation practices, its willingness to make scapegoats out of former employees and the arbitration system — run by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority — that everyone who deals with Wall Street is forced to use to resolve monetary disputes.

docs.snippet: The fashion house’s fall/winter 2014 couture runway earlier today had its share of standout moments, including one intricately embroidered minidress.
docs.lead_paragraph: The mood at today’s Valentino fall/winter 2014 couture show was par-for-the-course romantic. The wood-plank runway bedecked with moss and branches suggested a mythical forest to arriving guests, and what followed was a dance of ethereal, fairy-tale-like fashion moments. Subtle ballet references danced throughout the collection: leather belts on many of the looks mimicked the wraparound leotards worn for warm-ups, while delicate, knee-high lace-up sandals evoked the ties of toe shoes. The muted, wearable collection had its share of standout moments, but it was hard to forget this intricately embroidered pleated wrap minidress that felt at once folkloric and resolutely modern.

headline.main: A Modern Fairy-Tale Dress at Valentino

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s amazing what joy good air-conditioning and a midnight movie can bring, and the Film Society of Lincoln Center’s series Freaky Fridays — a delightfully unsettling meeting of horror, kink and 35 millimeter running through August (albeit at 11 p.m.) — offers plenty. docs.abstract: “Competing Utopias,” an exhibition of Cold War-era artifacts, opens in Richard Neutra’s former home in Los Angeles.
docs.snippet: “Competing Utopias,” an exhibition of Cold War-era artifacts, opens in Richard Neutra’s former home in Los Angeles.
docs.lead_paragraph: Some 350 Cold War-era artifacts, including teacups, tables and surveillance equipment used by the East German secret police, have replaced most of the furnishings in the Neutra VDL Studio and Residences in Los Angeles for “Competing Utopias: An Experimental Installation of Cold War Modern Design From East and West in One Context,” opening to the public on Sunday. It takes a disorienting look at the parallel universes on either side of the Iron Curtain, a “Twilight Zone”-like scenario where everything is the same — except that it’s different. “The similarity of objects from the East and West are pretty remarkable,” said Bill Ferehawk, who organized the show with Justinian Jampol, founder of the Wende Museum and Archive of the Cold War, and Sarah Lorenzen, the VDL House’s director. They use no labels, so unless visitors consult the iPads in the room, only clues like German phrases on coffee cans will hint at the décor’s origins. As Ms. Lorenzen said: “We want people to wonder: ‘How is history manufactured? How do stories get told? How different are we really?’ ” Through Sept. 13; neutra-vdl.org.

headline.main: Where the Curtains Were Made of Iron

docs.abstract: “The Living Landscape” gorgeously presents the many-layered life of the garden.
docs.snippet: “The Living Landscape” gorgeously presents the many-layered life of the garden.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a lot of talk about habitat gardens, but how many gardeners have watched a zebra swallowtail butterfly laying its eggs on a pawpaw leaf and then noticed the fuzzy larvae feeding on the leaves, which contain compounds that make the swallowtails unpalatable to birds? Two giants of the natural gardening world, Rick Darke and Doug Tallamy, have collaborated on their best work yet, “The Living Landscape: Designing for Beauty and Biodiversity in the Home Garden” (Timber Press, $39.95). It documents the layers and creatures of a healthy landscape, like ants carrying seeds of bloodroot and trillium back to their nests, and the blue-gray gnatcatcher nesting in a beech. Mr. Darke, a photographer as well as a plantsman and designer, took most of the gorgeous images, though Mr. Tallamy, an ecologist, offers inspiring close-ups of bugs and birds.

She nixed a few of Ms. Brito’s wilder ideas, like a bright red pendant lamp in the entry, and insisted on retaining some dull but ergonomic desk chairs. “Catherine is afraid of color,” Ms. Brito said with a smile.

docs.lead_paragraph: It was the greatest coffee run in American history. The Ohio boys had been fighting since morning, trapped in the raging battle of Antietam, in September 1862. Suddenly, a 19-year-old William McKinley appeared, under heavy fire, hauling vats of hot coffee. The men held out tin cups, gulped the brew and started firing again. “It was like putting a new regiment in the fight,” their officer recalled. Three decades later, McKinley ran for president in part on this singular act of caffeinated heroism.

headline.main: How Coffee Fueled the Civil War

Plovers hop around the frothy shore and small, see-through jellyfish float by, but the chefs are not distracted. docs.lead_paragraph: “The largest and arguably most effective antipoverty effort in the world is financed by the poor themselves,” writes The New York Times editorial board. “Last year alone, migrants in rich countries sent an estimated $404 billion to their families in developing countries.” Known as remittances, these transfers could see a rise in transfer fees as big banks like Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase are leaving the money-transfer business. Bankers claim “regulation has become too onerous in the wake of recent settlements over money laundering” connected to remittance transfers. But The Times believes “banks want out because they face dwindling profits from cash transfers. Over the last five years, there has been a successful global effort to lower remittance costs through greater transparency, better technology and other innovations.” If banks can’t profitably transmit remittances, “then other secure, low-cost options must be found.”

These were the first official acts of the ten-member cabinet after the 44-year-old Mr. Tshombe presented the ministers formally to President Joseph Kasavubu. docs.snippet: Online tutorials have opened the art of origami to a new generation of fans weaned on the Internet.
docs.lead_paragraph: PASADENA, Calif. — Robert J. Lang is one of the world’s foremost masters of origami. A former laser physicist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Mr. Lang ditched his day job at a fiber-optics company 13 years ago to devote his life to folding paper. Dozens of his featherweight creations are on display here at the Art Center College of Design: a peregrine falcon and an emperor scorpion, a stag beetle and a bull moose, all fashioned with such skill and lifelike detail, they appear ready to leap off their pristine white pedestals. The complex pieces require days of work and hundreds to thousands of folds. Viewers spend as much time enjoying their beauty as they do marveling at just how these animal figures were made, without cuts or glue, from a single sheet of paper.

headline.main: In Time-Lapse Videos, the Magic Unfolds

docs.abstract: Sleep does so much more for our bodies than preventing us from being tired tomorrow, but most parents don’t tell our children that. Educating kids about the importance of sleep leads them to sleep more.
docs.snippet: Sleep does so much more for our bodies than preventing us from being tired tomorrow, but most parents don’t tell our children that. Educating kids about the importance of sleep leads them to sleep more.
docs.lead_paragraph: We tell children why it’s important to eat their vegetables. We tell them why they need to get outside and run around. But how often do we parents tell children why it’s important to sleep? “Time for bed!” is usually the end of it, or maybe “You’ll be tired tomorrow.” No wonder children regard sleep as vaguely punitive, an enforced period of dull isolation in a darkened room. But of course sleep is so much more, and maybe we ought to try telling children that.

headline.main: We Tell Kids to ‘Go to Sleep!’ We Need to Teach Them Why.

As part of the Lincoln Center Festival, the company presents “Swan Lake” on Tuesday with David Hallberg — the first American to become a permanent member of the Bolshoi — and the gloriously willowy Svetlana Zakharova. After “Swan Lake,” which runs through next Sunday, are “Don Quixote” (July 22 and 23) and “Spartacus” (July 25 to 27). Since the productions lean toward the musty side — Yuri Grigorovich, the company’s former artistic director, choreographed both “Swan Lake” and “Spartacus” — it might be best to focus on the dancers. Along with Mr. Hallberg and Ms. Zakharova, there is the young Olga Smirnova, who performs “Swan Lake” opposite Semyon Chudin  next Saturday and next Sunday, and the boldly enticing Maria Alexandrova as Kitri in “Don Quixote” on July 22. As for “Spartacus”? It pretty much rains men. Leave your umbrella at home. (Tuesday through July 27; 212-721-6500, lincolncenterfestival.org.

docs.lead_paragraph: The first shot in “Boyhood,” Richard Linklater’s tender, profound film, is of a cloudy sky. The second is of a boy staring up at that sky, one arm bent under his head, the other flung out straight on the ground. He’s a pretty child with calm eyes, a snub nose and a full mouth. It’s a face that you get to know and love because, even as this child is watching the world, you’re watching him grow. In her comprehensive takedown, the historian Deirdre N. McCloskey noted that Clark’s idea was a “bold hypothesis, and was bold when first articulated by social Darwinists such as Charles Davenport and Francis Galton in the century before last.” Indeed, over the past 150 years, various white Western scientists and writers have repeatedly offered biological explanations for Caucasian superiority. docs.lead_paragraph: On a trip to Lusaka, Zambia, last year, I kept chasing an energetic and jittery Chinese man, the only staff member of a Chinese mining company willing to talk to me after his firm had been involved in several scandals in which both Chinese and Zambian employees were either killed or injured on the job. Zambia, with its abundant copper ore deposits, is one of the most important investment destinations for China. His English was excellent, and he liked to talk — and talk. After telling me about how much he loved the country and its people, he sometimes went into a rant about how Zambian miners liked drinking and money too much, and did not like to work hard. It was that mentality, he continued, that had caused his company all its troubles (not the workplace-safety and low-pay grievances of which it was accused). But even though the Zambian government had repossessed his company’s mines, this man wasn’t leaving. He was now working as an interpreter for the government.

docs.lead_paragraph: Four teenagers winning an academic contest might not seem to merit a documentary. Happens all the time, right? But in “Underwater Dreams,” the teenagers are Latinos — and illegal immigrants, four of the many who could gain citizenship through the Dream Act — from a low-income high school in Arizona. They win against many colleges, including M.I.T., in a robotics challenge. And their unlikely achievement, in 2004, reverberates a decade later, helping the students who followed them at Carl Hayden Community High School to have more confidence and even, in some cases, propelling them to work as engineers and as leaders in Dreamer groups.

docs.abstract: The Danish-American architect Knud Lonberg-Holm belonged to that moment in the 1920s when de Stijl principles were translated into three-dimensional space.
docs.snippet: The Danish-American architect Knud Lonberg-Holm belonged to that moment in the 1920s when de Stijl principles were translated into three-dimensional space.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Danish-American architect Knud Lonberg-Holm, the first European to teach the Bauhaus curriculum in America, belonged to that white-hot, manifesto-propelled moment in the 1920s when de Stijl principles were being translated into three-dimensional space. A dozen of his limpid gouache renderings of Michigan houses, all masterly compositions of point, line and plane, show buildings broken into constituent walls, roofs, floors and columns. With a palette of photographic black, white and gray, accented in blues and reds, he created weightless abstractions; solids and voids intersect in optical puzzles. He brushed calligraphic proposals for the new streamlined building types of the Machine Age — gas and radio stations — with a fierce graphic energy. His radically angled photographs of America’s traffic jams, skyscrapers, fire escapes and power lines found their way into “Amerika,” the German architect Erich Mendelsohn’s photographic essay of American cityscapes. Letters from Theo van Doesburg, Walter Gropius and Mies van der Rohe authenticate his position as a peer. Buckminster Fuller wanted to write a book about him.

headline.main: Knud Lonberg-Holm: ‘The Invisible Architect’

docs.abstract: “Help!,” Dan Colen’s show at the Brant Foundation in Greenwich, Conn., recalls a friend and muse who died young.
docs.snippet: “Help!,” Dan Colen’s show at the Brant Foundation in Greenwich, Conn., recalls a friend and muse who died young.
docs.lead_paragraph: At the grassy summit of a low hill outside the Brant Foundation Art Study Center in Greenwich, Conn., the metal cargo containers of two 14-foot box trucks rise vertically like twin towers, their cabs buried underground. It’s a sculpture called “At Least They Died Together (After Dash)” (2013-14), by Dan Colen, and it’s a memorial to his friend Dash Snow, who died of a drug overdose in 2009. It appears as an incongruous eyesore against the backdrop of its bucolic surroundings. Visitors may notice that the thin skins of the truck boxes have holes in them. During the exhibition’s opening, Mr. Colen threw rocks and hammers at them, while drummers of the two-person band I.U.D. — one atop each of the truck ends — played thunderously.

headline.main: Ashes to Ashes, Dust to Powder

docs.lead_paragraph: Secretary General Ban Ki-moon announced Thursday that he had appointed Staffan de Mistura, a veteran diplomat of Italian-Swedish heritage who has led United Nations missions in Iraq and Afghanistan, to be the new special envoy responsible for seeking an end to the conflict in Syria. Mr. Ban said Mr. de Mistura, whose appointment had been expected by other diplomats, would be working to stop “all violence and human rights violations, and promoting a peaceful solution to the Syrian crisis.” Mr. de Mistura’s predecessor, Lakhdar Brahimi, resigned two months ago in frustration. He had replaced Kofi Annan, the former secretary general who called the Syria job “mission impossible.” Mr. Ban also said that he had appointed Ramzy Ezzeldin Ramzy, an Egyptian diplomat, as Mr. de Mistura’s deputy.

docs.abstract: Just a few minutes on a grill brings out juices and warms up summer fruit like peaches, apricots and watermelon, which can served simply with a honey and lemon zest, or used in salads and crêpes.
docs.snippet: Just a few minutes on a grill brings out juices and warms up summer fruit like peaches, apricots and watermelon, which can served simply with a honey and lemon zest, or used in salads and crêpes.
docs.lead_paragraph: On the Fourth of July, before the meat and fish hit the grill, I decided to throw on some fruit. I’ve always loved the way roasting summer stone fruit like peaches and apricots deepens their flavors, and I thought a sizzle on the grill might do the same. It did. Just a few minutes on each side – enough to create griddle marks on a peach or an apricot and soften it, but not so long that the fruit collapses, brought out the juices and warmed the fruit through. When I removed the peaches and apricots from the grill I tossed them with a little honey and lemon zest.

headline.main: These Fruits Were Made for Grilling

docs.lead_paragraph: 8 P.M. (Starz) FROZEN (2013) Warm up your vocal cords. This Disney 3-D animated movie musical produced “Let It Go,” the Oscar-winning power anthem, written by Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez, on seemingly every child’s (and quite a few adults’) lips since its release in November. Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee directed this fable about Elsa (the voice of Idina Menzel), an ice princess cursed with a frigid touch, and Anna (Kristen Bell), her younger sister and best friend. When Anna falls for a handsome prince (Santino Fontana), Elsa forbids them to marry, casting their Scandinavian kingdom into eternal winter with a wave of her hand. Horrified, she retreats to an ice palace atop a mountain, but sibling love sends Anna plowing through drifts and up glacial ridges in search of Elsa, confident that she can reverse the spell. “Allegorically, ‘Frozen’ lacks the purity and elemental power of a classic myth like ‘Beauty and the Beast,’ but at least its storytelling is fairly coherent, and its gleaming dream world of snow and ice is one of the most visually captivating environments to be found in a Disney animated film,” Stephen Holden wrote in The New York Times about this blockbuster, inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Snow Queen.” “There are moments when you may feel that you are inside a giant crystal chandelier frosted with diamonds.” Josh Gad plays Olaf, the snowman sidekick (above, with Anna and Kristoff, voiced by Jonathan Groff) who would rather be a beach bunny, in this Oscar winner for best animated feature.
