docs.abstract: Black and white, young and old, billionaires and shop owners — a growing chorus of optimists in Detroit is saying that the time is right to invest.
docs.snippet: Black and white, young and old, billionaires and shop owners — a growing chorus of optimists in Detroit is saying that the time is right to invest.
docs.lead_paragraph: In downtown Detroit, at the headquarters of the online-mortgage company Quicken Loans, there stands another downtown Detroit in miniature. The diorama, made of laser-cut acrylic and stretching out over 19 feet in length, is a riot of color and light: Every structure belonging to Quicken’s billionaire owner, Dan Gilbert, is topped in orange and illuminated from within, and Gilbert currently owns 60 of them, a lordly nine million square feet of real estate in all. He began picking up skyscrapers just three and a half years ago, one after another, paying as little as $8 a square foot. He bought five buildings surrounding Capitol Park, the seat of government when Michigan became a state in 1837. He snapped up the site of the old Hudson’s department store, where 12,000 employees catered to 100,000 customers daily in the 1950s. Many of Gilbert’s purchases are 20th-century architectural treasures, built when Detroit served as a hub of world industry. He bought a Daniel Burnham, a few Albert Kahns, a Minoru Yamasaki masterwork with a soaring glass atrium. “They’re like old-school sports cars,” said Dan Mullen, one of the executives who took over Quicken’s newly formed real estate arm. “These were buildings with so much character, so much history. They don’t exist anywhere else. And it was like, ‘Buy this parking garage, and we’ll throw in a skyscraper with it.’ ”

headline.main: The Post-Post-Apocalyptic Detroit
headline.print_headline: Buy Low

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: France celebrates Bastille Day in 1964.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: France celebrates Bastille Day in 1964.
docs.lead_paragraph: PARIS — The huge doors of firehouses throughout the city swung open this afternoon and thousands of Parisians invaded gaily decorated courtyards to start off the annual dance marathon coinciding with the anniversary of the fall of the Bastille. By tomorrow evening, scores of competing “bals” will have sprung up at most of the major intersections and squares, and seemingly nearly all of Paris will be kicking high in a polka or weaving in a conga line. With a frenzy matching the revolutionary fervor in the streets on July 14, 1789, many will pursue the dancing until dawn on Tuesday. The hardiest then will rest briefly before hustling over to the Champs-Élysées for the annual military parade. Officially, July 14 has been celebrated as a national holiday only since 1880. The parliament then, it has been said, wanted to endow the Third Republic with a fête day comparable to those established under previous regimes. Although nearly a century had passed since the Revolution, strong but futile protests were delivered in parliament against the official glorification of a day associated with the parading of decapitated heads on spikes in the streets. Some of the rites marking that first official commemoration continue to be observed today. Others have been modified or have disappeared. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 13, 1964

headline.main: 1964: Dance Marathon in Paris

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The British Royal Air Force stages a sham air raid in 1939.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The British Royal Air Force stages a sham air raid in 1939.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — More than 120 of the finest heavy and medium bombers of the British Royal Air Force participated today [July 11] in the most impressive and significant sham air raid yet staged in air-conscious Europe. Taking off in succession this morning from their aerodrome in the English Midlands, the British planes pointed southward and “spread their wings” out over France. Never before had so many military planes of one country carried out an expedition of this character over the territory of another. The only information given the squadron commanders before they left the ground was that their destinations were “somewhere in France.” Sealed orders, when broken in the air, instructed the heavy bombers, totaling about eighty units, to make a round- trip, non-stop flight to Bordeaux, the French port on the Bay of Biscay, a two- way distance of nearly 1,200 miles. Similar orders provided a shorter flight for about forty medium bombers passing above the French cities of Le Treport, Orleans, and Le Mans, near Cherbourg. Their cruising radius is more restricted. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 12, 1939

Judith Viorst (“Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day”) and the late Charlotte Zolotow (“The Hating Book,” “William’s Doll”) proved to be masters of the genre, their dry-eyed wit, empathic touch and storytelling prowess easily a match for their good intentions.

docs.abstract: A classicist tries to unravel the enigma of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher who tutored the emperor Nero.
docs.snippet: A classicist tries to unravel the enigma of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher who tutored the emperor Nero.
docs.lead_paragraph: The name Seneca brings a particular image to mind: a gaunt, half-naked old man, glaring wildly, his veins open, his lifeblood seeping into the small bath beneath him after he was forced to commit suicide. Painted by Rubens, memorialized by Dante in his first circle of hell, gilded into medieval manuscripts alongside Plato and Aristotle, Seneca has come to represent the perils of proximity to absolute power. The central question of James Romm’s “Dying Every Day” is this: When we confront this tragic Roman wordsmith, tutor to the emperor Nero (and, some argue, the power behind that terrible throne), who stares back at us? Is it a tyrannodidaskalos, a tyrant-teacher? Is he the ultimate exemplar of Stoicism, a would-be philosopher king? Or is Seneca simply an accretion of history, a phantom constructed to fit our ravening for heroes, for antiheroes and for the sensational in the stories of antiquity?

docs.abstract: Joan Rivers’s “Diary of a Mad Diva,” No. 7 on the hardcover nonfiction list, is filled with the author’s brand of rapid-fire politically incorrect jokes.
docs.snippet: Joan Rivers’s “Diary of a Mad Diva,” No. 7 on the hardcover nonfiction list, is filled with the author’s brand of rapid-fire politically incorrect jokes.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Fur Flies: Comedy is like sex, or subatomic particles: The more you try to analyze it, the more elusive it becomes. So it’s probably futile to look too closely at Joan Rivers’s latest book, “Diary of a Mad Diva,” new at No. 7 on the hardcover nonfiction list. But what the heck. As its title suggests, the book is structured as a conventional diary that happens to be filled with the author’s brand of rapid-fire politically incorrect jokes — in the second entry, Rivers contrasts herself favorably with Anne Frank: “I’ve written six books, and Anne? She didn’t even complete her one.” Rivers is unavoidably outré — racist, sexist, raunchy, crass — which isn’t to everybody’s taste. (Another way comedy resembles sex, and maybe subatomic particles — I’m no scientist — is that different folks like different strokes.) But readers seem divided as to whether Rivers is truly meanspirited or whether it’s all a provocation, a persona she slips into as easily as the fur coat she’s wearing on her book’s cover. When the CNN anchor Fredricka Whitfield suggested as much in a recent interview, noting that Rivers is a well-known animal rights advocate and wondering whether the fur was there just for its shock value, Rivers went ballistic. “Are you wearing leather shoes? Then shut up,” she said, before storming off the set. “I don’t want to hear this nonsense.” She didn’t seem to be joking.

docs.lead_paragraph: Ask most travelers about Austrian cities beyond Vienna, and you’ll probably hear suggestions to go to Salzburg or Innsbruck. Austrians, however, might tell you that Graz — their country’s second-largest city, with a population of just over 300,000 — is a better choice for many tourists, thanks to its rich design, art and culinary scenes, and wine and produce from the surrounding south Austrian state of Styria. Built around the Schlossberg, an ancient hilltop castle, Styria’s regional capital is home to scores of boutiques, shops, restaurants and museums, many housed in restored Baroque-era buildings in the city’s well-preserved Old Town. You might not expect to find such a cultivated metropolis two hours down the road from Vienna toward Ljubljana, but Graz has a palpable joie de vivre, thanks in part to the presence of its six universities and over 40,000 students.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Land Ho!,” Martha Stephens and Aaron Katz’s sweet and often hilarious road film about a pair of older men who travel to Iceland to reclaim their youth, began as something far less ambitious. “I wanted to go on a vacation to Iceland,” says Stephens, whose first two films, “Passenger Pigeons” and “Pilgrim Song,” were well-received indie outings. As she researched her trip, however, Stephens saw the opportunity to use the country’s breathtaking landscapes for a more creative purpose. She enlisted Katz, the director of the mumblecore favorites “Dance Party USA” and “Quiet City,” whom she knew from the University of North Carolina School of the Arts, to help write the script and co-direct, and the pair cast Stephens’s second cousin, Earl Lynn Nelson, an oculoplastic surgeon, and the indie actor Paul Eenhoorn (“This Is Martin Bonner”), as the film’s jocular leads, Mitch and Colin.

headline.main: The Directors of “Land Ho!” On Their Icelandic Adventure

Mr. Long lives in West Brighton, Staten Island, with his wife, Nina, 59, and his daughters, Katrina, 34; Madeline, 26; and Emily, 21.

docs.lead_paragraph: Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Friday outlined his vision for his presidential campaign, promising to expand rights and liberties, improve welfare programs and build up Turkey’s economy. On Aug. 10, for the first time, Turkey’s president will be chosen directly by the voters, rather than by Parliament. The presidency has been largely a ceremonial post, but if Mr. Erdogan wins, as is widely expected, he is likely to try to expand the powers of the office. Mr. Erdogan has been the most powerful figure in Turkish politics for a decade. His opponents fear that if he is elected president, he will face no checks on the autocratic tendencies he has displayed in recent months while confronting challenges from street protests and a corruption inquiry. Speaking to more than two thousand supporters in Istanbul on Friday, Mr. Erdogan offered few details but vowed to expand democracy in Turkey if elected and to expand its role in international affairs.

headline.main: Turkey: Prime Minister Looks Ahead

docs.abstract: The number of South Sudanese fleeing for neighboring nations has reached 715,000, the United Nations refugee agency said, amid a civil war and the threat of famine.
docs.snippet: The number of South Sudanese fleeing for neighboring nations has reached 715,000, the United Nations refugee agency said, amid a civil war and the threat of famine.
docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations refugee agency said Friday that the number of South Sudanese fleeing for neighboring nations is expected to reach as many as 715,000 by year’s end, more than double the number envisioned when the agency began a funding appeal four months ago for refugees from South Sudan, which has been ravaged by a civil war and is on the verge of famine. “The ongoing conflict and worsening humanitarian situation inside the world’s youngest nation is fueling a refugee exodus into Ethiopia, Kenya, Sudan and Uganda at a much higher rate than initially anticipated,” an agency spokeswoman, Melissa Fleming, said in a statement on the crisis in South Sudan. The agency revised its funding appeal to $658 million from the original $371 million and warned that without urgent contributions, “the consequences could be drastic.” In another barometer of the worsening crisis, the charity Save the Children warned that a cholera outbreak that first appeared two months ago had spread, infecting more than 2,600 people and killing more than 60. Pete Walsh, Save the Children’s director in South Sudan, said in a statement that the country’s overstretched health service was plagued by widespread shortages of lifesaving supplies, as “desperate parents are coming to clinics with children who are already considerably weakened by the disease.”

headline.main: South Sudan: Refugee Crisis Worsens

docs.abstract: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: a perilous ascent in Switzerland in 1914 by Mr. J. H. Brady.
docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: a perilous ascent in Switzerland in 1914 by Mr. J. H. Brady.
docs.lead_paragraph: LITTLE SCHEIDEGG, Switzerland – The ascent of the Mönch made on Saturday by Mr. J. H. Brady, of Baltimore, was accomplished in face of the most unfavorable conditions, and the route chosen on the northern side of the peak was one of the most difficult. The progress of Mr. Brady and the two Grindelwald guides, Christian and Peter Kaufmann, who accompanied him, could be observed nearly all the time through glasses from the Seiler Hotel, at Little Scheidegg. The party took ten hours to reach the summit. The ascent of the Mönch peak, although its altitude is not quite as great as that of the Jungfrau, is one of the most difficult climbs in the Bernese Oberland. From Little Scheidegg, at the foot of the Eiger — which with the Mönch and the Jungfrau forms the Interlaken group of peaks, of which the Mönch is the central one — the journey requires at least thirteen hours, with a stop for rest and sleep at the Guggi Hut, where climbers for the Mönch and the Jungfrau part company. The Mönch was first scaled by Dr. Porges, of Vienna, in 1857. Its altitude is 13,465 feet, and the climb from the Guggi requires between nine and ten hours. It cannot be undertaken by anyone but a most experienced climber, as the difficulties to be overcome are innumerable. — The New York Herald, European Edition, July 14, 1914

headline.main: 1914: Brady Climbs The Mönch in Just Ten Hours

docs.abstract: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: New bill in England bans revengeful wills in 1939.
docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: New bill in England bans revengeful wills in 1939.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON – One of the foundations of English law — that a person of sound mind may will his property to whom he likes — was set aside today [July 13] by the inheritance family provision act which came into operation in the British Isles. The act provides for nullification by court order of revengeful wills in which husbands or wives cut off their widow or widowers and children with a contemptuous shilling or nothing at all, leaving them destitute while the money goes to charity, to persons outside the family or to some freakish cause. Testators are given self-defense, however, in a clause permitting them to append a side statement to their wills setting forth the reason for ignoring the dependants. The courts will take such a statement into consideration when dealing with a contested will. Those who may benefit under the act are limited to a widow or widower, unmarried daughters of any age, sons under twenty-one and sons or daughters who cannot earn their living because of mental or physical incapacity. If any such persons contest a will, a court will decide whether ‘‘reasonable provision’’ has been made. If not, the court may ‘‘tear up’’ the will and redistribute the assets of an estate. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 14, 1939

headline.main: 1939: England Bans Revengeful Wills

Malcolm Reynolds (Nathan Fillion) tries to scrape together a living smuggling cargo from one fringe of the universe to the next in this film written and directed by Joss Whedon. But the crew members’ off-the-radar existence is threatened when an agent (Chiwetel Ejiofor) of an oppressive government tracks them down, intent on killing a teenager aboard the ship (Summer Glau, above). Writing in The New York Times, Manohla Dargis compared this science-fiction adventure with the “Star Wars” movies by George Lucas. “Scene for scene, ‘Serenity’ is more engaging and certainly better written and acted than any of Mr. Lucas’s recent screen entertainments,” she wrote. “Mr. Whedon isn’t aiming to conquer the pop-culture universe with a branded mythology; he just wants us to hitch a ride to a galaxy far, far away and have a good time.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Christopher Walken, below, will grab the hammy role of Captain Hook in NBC’s new live version of “Peter Pan,” the network’s follow-up to its hugely successful live musical for this past holiday season, “The Sound of Music.” Robert Greenblatt, NBC’s top entertainment executive, announced the casting of Mr. Walken on Sunday in Los Angeles at an annual gathering of television critics. Mr. Greenblatt cited Mr. Walken’s early experience as a song-and-dance man as well as his numerous well-received appearances as a guest host of “Saturday Night Live.” NBC plans to mount the production, “Peter Pan Live!,” in December. The network still needs to find a Peter. Mr. Greenblatt had no announcement on that front, although he did confirm that the network had pursued Kristen Bell (“Frozen”), but could not work out a schedule for her because of her commitment to the Showtime series “House of Lies.” Mr. Greenblatt did say that NBC would stick to the tradition of hiring a female star for Peter, after originally thinking that a man might be considered for the part.

docs.lead_paragraph: Mario Correa’s political comedy “Tail! Spin!” is to open Off Broadway at the Lynn Redgrave Theater just as this fall’s midterm elections are heating up, the show’s producers announced on Sunday. The play was warmly received at the 2012 New York International Fringe Festival. Dan Knechtges will return as director, and Rachel Dratch (“Saturday Night Live”) will reprise her roles as “Wives, Tails, Beards & Barbara Walters.” Other roles are expected to be cast this month, Billy Zavelson, one of the show’s producers, said by phone. “Tail! Spin!” uses texts, emails, tweets and remarks from four politicians disgraced by sex scandals: Anthony Weiner, Mark Foley, Larry Craig and Mark Sanford. It has been updated to include material from Mr. Weiner’s unsuccessful run for mayor of New York and Mr. Sanford’s election to Congress, Mr. Zavelson said. “And if another scandal of this ilk happens, we’ll add that to the show, too,” he said. “Tail! Spin!” is to begin previews on Sept. 18 and will open on Oct. 1.

headline.main: A Political Comedy for Off Broadway

docs.lead_paragraph: Much to the chagrin of women’s rights advocates, Hobby Lobby has won its legal battle — but claims of “victory” for religious freedom must be emended. Make no mistake: This is no victory for the freedom to exercise Christian principles. Though employers like Hobby Lobby are now free to deny women access to contraceptives through their employer-subsidized health plans on the basis of religious objection, they will be violating their own purported Christian principles if they do. While Christians are not compelled by their faith to engage in religious practices that impose upon the freedoms of others, they are compelled — by their belief that all persons, men and women, are created in the image of God — to oppose discrimination.

docs.lead_paragraph: I am at the Jardin des Plantes, in the Fifth Arrondissement on the Left Bank of the Seine. Here we find one of the world’s oldest zoos, still officially called a “menagerie,” various greenhouses and rows of brilliant dahlias book-ended by statues of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon. We also find the various galleries composing the National Museum of Natural History. docs.lead_paragraph: The tastefully designed, subtly scented candles of Maison Louis Marie continue to draw distinguished noses to the doorsteps of fashionable outposts like Fred Segal in Los Angeles and Assembly in New York, and all the Steven Alan stores across the country in between. And today, the Belgian behind the brand, Marie du Petit Thouars, introduces her first collection of personal fragrance oils, four of which borrow the delicate bouquet of some of her most coveted candles, and one of which is being introduced for the first time. “Each scent from my collection represents a person, place or memory of my family and childhood that is created through blends of notes that utilize vast arrays of the botanical world,” she says. Another of her dearest childhood memories inspired her to create the oils, four of which are unisex, in the first place. “I remember when I was a child, I went on a fishing trip in the Mauritius Islands with a master perfumer from the Guerlain family,” she says. “He had created a perfume inspired by a woman with whom he had fallen in love with and wanted to reveal her sensuality through a perfume. I was absolutely charmed by this — what a beautiful gift to be able to give someone.”

headline.main: A Coveted Candle Line Branches Out into Personal Perfumes

docs.abstract: Francophile chefs agree that this Provençal dish, perfect for sharing, is especially delicious in the summer months.
docs.snippet: Francophile chefs agree that this Provençal dish, perfect for sharing, is especially delicious in the summer months.
docs.lead_paragraph: On this, the anniversary of the storming of the Bastille, there may not be a more appropriate, or at least delicious, way to celebrate the values of liberté, égalité and fraternité than with the traditional Provençal feast, le grand aioli. The pungent emulsion referred to as “the butter of Provence” is predictably the hero of the meal; however, it is arguably its accompaniments that make it truly grand. Served in bowls or the heavy mortars in which it is made, the aioli becomes a centerpiece flanked by an array of whatever is best from the market that day. Languid, unstructured and designed for sharing, at its best le grand aioli is a celebration of summer’s bounty andesprit.

headline.main: Le Grand Aioli: a Culinary Ode to Bastille Day

I did not make any decision to become one. I did not, at the beginning, expect to earn a living by being read. I wrote as a child out of the joy of apprehending life through my senses — the look and scent and feel of things; and soon out of the emotions that puzzled me or raged within me and which took form, found some enlightenment, solace and delight, shaped in the written word.”

headline.main: Looking Back at Nadine Gordimer’s Life and Work

docs.lead_paragraph: LEOPOLDVILLE — Premier Moise Tshombe’s government today [July 14] invited the family of murdered premier Patrice Lumumba to return to the Congo from its voluntary exile in the United Arab Republic. Mrs. Lumumba and her four children left for Cairo in 1961 shortly after Mr. Lumumba was murdered in Katanga, where he had been sent for “safekeeping” by the Leopoldville authorities who ousted him from power. Mr. Tshombe, who was president of Katanga at the time, has been accused of complicity in Mr. Lumumba’s death. It was not immediately known whether Mr. Tshombe would attempt personally to persuade Mrs. Lumumba to return. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 15

headline.main: 1964: Offer of Return to Congo

docs.abstract: Is Mark Lilla right to describe ours as a “libertarian age”?
docs.snippet: Is Mark Lilla right to describe ours as a “libertarian age”?
docs.lead_paragraph: As an interlude between “reform conservatism and …” posts, I want to return to the Mark Lilla essay on our present political situation that I commented on a couple of weeks ago, this time to quibble a little bit with its title. That title is “The Truth About Our Libertarian Age,” and most writers I’ve seen commenting on the essay — from my colleague David Brooks to Andrew Sullivan to Damon Linker — have tended to basically accept Lilla’s formulation, which links the spread of cultural individualism (defined as “an outlook with treats as axiomatic the primacy of individual self-determination over traditional social ties”) to the durable triumph of neoliberalism in political economy, and places both under the umbrella of a libertarianism ascendant.

headline.main: On the Nature of Our Regime

docs.lead_paragraph: An Egyptian court on Monday lifted a ban that prevented members of the political party of former President Hosni Mubarak, who was ousted in 2011, from standing in parliamentary and local elections, state media reported. The court’s decision, which said that party members who had not been convicted of crimes should not be excluded from public life, appeared to pave the way for the rehabilitation of members of Egypt’s once-disgraced old guard. Mr. Mubarak’s National Democratic Party, which dominated politics for decades, was dissolved after his ouster. The Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist group that won successive elections after Mr. Mubarak’s fall, was swept from power during a military takeover of the government last year and banned as part of a crackdown on political opposition. Experts say a new election law is likely to further constrict Egypt’s political life, producing a legislature subservient to the new president, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, while reviving some of the patronage networks that thrived under Mr. Mubarak.

headline.main: Egypt: Opening for the Old Guard

docs.snippet: The Supreme Court of India on Monday temporarily stayed the execution of two men convicted of raping and murdering a 23-year-old woman on a bus in New Delhi in 2012, said their lawyer, A. P. Singh, in a case that drew international attention, prom...
docs.lead_paragraph: The Supreme Court of India on Monday temporarily stayed the execution of two men convicted of raping and murdering a 23-year-old woman on a bus in New Delhi in 2012, said their lawyer, A. P. Singh, in a case that drew international attention, prompted an outcry in India and led to the strengthening of sexual assault laws. The court on Monday stayed the executions of Vinay Sharma and Akshay Kumar Singh; the executions of two other defendants were also stayed by the Supreme Court in March after appeals were filed. All four were convicted of the crimes and sentenced to death last September. The district court that convicted the men categorized the case, in which the victim was repeatedly assaulted with iron rods on a moving bus, as the “rarest of the rare,” a designation that allowed the application of the death penalty. The four defendants plan to continue their appeals, and a final hearing is scheduled for August, said Manohar Lal Sharma, a lawyer for two of the defendants. Another accused, a juvenile at the time of the crime, was sentenced to three years in prison, and a sixth hanged himself in his prison cell.

headline.main: India: Court Stays Executions for 2 Convicted in Gang-Rape Case

docs.snippet: Secretary General Ban Ki-moon of the United Nations visited Haiti on Monday and sought to assure Haitians that he was committed to ending a cholera epidemic “as quickly as possible,” but he did not acknowledge his organization’s possible complicit...
docs.lead_paragraph: Secretary General Ban Ki-moon of the United Nations visited Haiti on Monday and sought to assure Haitians that he was committed to ending a cholera epidemic “as quickly as possible,” but he did not acknowledge his organization’s possible complicity in causing it, the subject of at least two lawsuits filed in the United States. In a speech in Los Palmas, a village ravaged by the disease, Mr. Ban called the visit “a necessary pilgrimage” that was aimed at expressing solidarity with the cholera victims. He has been seeking to raise $2.2 billion to eradicate cholera, which has killed more than 8,000 people in Haiti since 2010. It was absent from the country for nearly 100 years until after the January 2010 earthquake. Forensic studies have identified the cholera bacteria as an Asian strain carried by Nepalese members of a United Nations peacekeeping force in Haiti. Stanley N. Alpert, a lawyer representing Haitian victims in a lawsuit, called the secretary general’s speech “devoid of any sense of responsibility for the fact that the U.N. brought the cholera to Haiti and it should have gone into overdrive to shut it down.”

headline.main: Haiti: A U.N. Cholera ‘Pilgrimage’

docs.lead_paragraph: Just before the rush of dinner service, the pastry chef Brooks Headley agreed to serve me a veggie burger at Del Posto’s gleaming marble bar in Chelsea. In the mid-’90s, when Headley played drums with the Young Pioneers, he loved veggie burgers so much that he planned the punk band’s tours around stops at Faque Burger in San Diego for the vegetarian diner’s soy-based patty. He’s still obsessed. He has served his own veggie burger to David Chang, who posted a close-up to Instagram (1.8K likes), declaring it the best he’s ever tried. Questlove asked Headley to serve the burger at his food salon. And this Sunday, the guy who turned the most profoundly uncool snack on the planet into something sought after will serve his patties to the public at his first pop-up, Superiority Burger on the Lower East Side.

docs.lead_paragraph: In early 1864, the Union Army began enlisting black soldiers in Kentucky, but Capt. J. Bates Dickson, an enlistment officer in the state, didn’t expect much – they might come “singly and in squads,” but not waves. Indeed, despite tens of thousands of fighting-age black men in the state, turnout was paltry – after all, Kentucky was still a slave state, and enlistment was restricted to free blacks and to slaves whose owners permitted them to go. Most slaveholders and their allies resisted black enlistment by any means possible, often with cruelty and violence.

headline.main: A ‘Stampede’ for Freedom

docs.lead_paragraph: In Somerset, an English county marked by rolling farmland, the new and much-anticipated Hauser & Wirth outpost finally opened its doors today. T first profiled the project in April, in the Spring Design 2014 issue, with a first look at the arts center being carved out of a working farm there. The story focused on the farmhouse at Durslade Farm, a property that had been abandoned for 10 years and then left untouched for 50 before being restored and renovated by the Paris-based architect Luis Laplace. Its six guest bedrooms were then filled with pieces by Hauser & Wirth’s impressive lineup of artists, including Pipilotti Rist and Paul McCarthy, and the grounds were landscaped by none other than Piet Oudolf, the Dutch garden designer behind home-like public gardens such as the High Line in Manhattan.

docs.abstract: Alex Butler’s new verse volume, “Circling the Same” — which she’ll read from tonight at Creatures of Comfort — is a multimedia experience.
docs.snippet: Alex Butler’s new verse volume, “Circling the Same” — which she’ll read from tonight at Creatures of Comfort — is a multimedia experience.
docs.lead_paragraph: The writer Alex Butler may live in brownstone Brooklyn, but that’s about the extent of her similarities to the young literary set. A licensed social worker, she has also worked for the designer Jane Mayle, served as a production assistant on the set of “Sex and the City” and recorded a series of humorous performance videos. It was the loss, in quick succession, of both her parents — and Butler’s experience as her mother’s caretaker during a harrowing illness — that spurred her to turn what had been a secret hobby into a career. But rather than sit down at a laptop and type about the experience, she began speaking words and dialogue into a Dictaphone — and later her computer’s camera — which led to not one, but two books: her debut memoir, “Walking the Night Road,” due out next year from Columbia University Press, and “Circling the Same,” a 41-poem meditation on loss. The latter — newly available online through its publisher, the Los Angeles–based gallery and art-book press Ohwow — is as much art object as literature: Butler’s words are printed alongside photographs from the artists Mirabelle Marden and Andrea Longacre-White. “Both of these artists’ work, and what I imagined were their intentions, reminded me of a world altered by grief,” she explains.

headline.main: Introducing a Poet Who Works in 3-D

docs.lead_paragraph: A powerful storm cut through the Philippines on Wednesday morning, killing at least one person and sending more than 150,000 people into shelters, disaster response officials said. Typhoon Rammasun caused landslides and flooding along its path from the central Philippines to the northern peninsula of Bataan, passing just south of the capital city, Manila. Government rescue teams were trying to reach remote areas south of Manila affected by the storm, which packed winds of 90 miles per hour and gusts to 115 miles an hour. The one confirmed fatality as of Wednesday morning involved a woman being hit by a falling electric pole, officials said. Last November, Typhoon Haiyan, one of the strongest storms on record, devastated the islands of Leyte and Samar on the east coast and killed more than 6,300 people.

headline.main: Philippines: A Deadly Typhoon

docs.abstract: Parents trying to administer medicine to children younger than 12 are often baffled by measuring options and confusing labels.
docs.snippet: Parents trying to administer medicine to children younger than 12 are often baffled by measuring options and confusing labels.
docs.lead_paragraph: Parents trying to administer medicine to children younger than 12 are often baffled by such options for measuring as milliliters, milligrams, teaspoons, tablespoons and droppers. In A Spoonful of Medicine May Put Children at Risk Jan Hoffman describes new efforts by professional associations to persuade manufacturers and pharmacists to adopt a uniform unit for liquid medicines: the milliliter. She describes the mistakes in dosing made by parents grabbing kitchen spoons, confusing teaspoons and tablespoons, and misreading instructions. Of 287 parents interviewed shortly after they had finished giving medication to their children that had been prescribed at the emergency departments at Bellevue Hospital Center in Manhattan and Woodhull Medical Center in Brooklyn, more than 40 percent of the parents had not measured correctly.

headline.main: Simplifying Measuring Medication for Children

docs.lead_paragraph: PARIS — The world reacted emphatically to Barry Goldwater today and most of the reaction was hostile. From London to Paris to Bonn to Moscow, commentators denounced the Arizona senator as a reactionary and a cold-warmonger. Only in Madrid and Johannesburg and a few other cities were voices of approval raised as the news flashed around the world of the senator’s nomination as the Republican presidential candidate. In London, the pro-Labor mass-circulation “Daily Mirror” said: “The corpse of much that is decent and wise and tolerant in American society is in the coffin, although the lid has not yet finally been screwed down.” — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 17, 1964

headline.main: 1964: Hostility Shown to Goldwater

docs.lead_paragraph: Even in his mid-1960s heyday, Bert Berns was barely known beyond the obsessives who studied songwriters’ and producers’ credits on 45 r.p.m. records and LP album jackets. And then, after his death in 1967 at the age of 38, something truly odd happened: Though the songs he wrote and produced, like “Twist and Shout” and “Hang On Sloopy,” proved to have durability, growing in stature and popularity as the years passed, Berns’s own reputation receded even further into obscurity.

docs.abstract: Returning to New York after nine years, the Bolshoi Ballet is presenting three works at the Lincoln Center Festival.

docs.lead_paragraph: Returning to New York after nine years, the Bolshoi Ballet — the most heroically warm-blooded of ballet companies — seems keen to prove that it has reverted to the ghastly artistic torpor it enjoyed in the last two decades of the Soviet era. For a short time this century (thanks principally to the choreographer Alexei Ratmansky, who was for a few years its artistic director), this flagship company became an important center of new choreography and home to major revivals that changed Russia’s and the world’s view of dance history. But the three productions that it’s showing as part of the Lincoln Center Festival, all deriving from an earlier era, have been seen here before — a lot — and none of them are good.

docs.snippet: Buddy Warren, a psychologist-turned-decorator, has a new design shop on the Lower East Side.
docs.lead_paragraph: No question, Buddy Warren’s first Manhattan antiques store, Cranberry Hole Road, was an original. It had a coffee bar downstairs and a place for Mr. Warren to conduct family therapy sessions upstairs. That boutique closed in 2004, but the psychologist-turned-interior-decorator-and-licensed-contractor is back with another retail adventure. His new self-named shop (left photo) sits in a 19th-century building on the Lower East Side that began life as a barn. About a third of the items are Mr. Warren’s own concoctions, like an iron cage table with a base sliced from an 18th-century marble column and a glass top ($950, seen in right photo). The rest ranges from cleansing bars made by a New Hampshire beekeeper ($6) to authentic Windsor chairs ($14,000 for a set of eight). Coffee is still served, but upstairs is now for workshops on themes like organization. 171 Chrystie Street (Rivington Street). Information: 212-727-8400 or buddywarren.com.

docs.lead_paragraph: Maria Bamford has a mantra of sorts, and here it is: Do the work. Three words, three syllables. An easy, orderly thing. She tells it to herself when she wakes up in the morning, whether it’s at her bungalow in a middle-class neighborhood on the outskirts of Los Angeles or at a Holiday Inn in Boston or a Marriott in Bloomington, or any of the other highway-side hotels she hits for one night before moving on. Do the work. It’s a stay against paralysis, against the descent of dread. It’s less dramatic than “seize the day!” more affirming than “stop overthinking everything!” It is functional, and that’s what she’s trying to be. Do the work. She repeats it on airplanes, in taxis, on the long walks she takes to calm her nerves before a show. Sometimes she amends it to: Just do the work, the “just” a reminder that she’s not, after all, performing surgery on babies. There’s another, more refined version, too. Do your bits, she’ll tell herself, resigned to the idea that this may always be a struggle. Just do your bits.

headline.main: The Weird, Scary and Ingenious Brain of Maria Bamford

docs.lead_paragraph: As a supplement to my last post, which ended by discussing some of the difficulties inherent in devising a point-by-point foreign policy agenda – difficulties that the horrific news from Ukraine throw into sharp relief – let me quote from a new essay from The American Conservative’s editor, Daniel McCarthy, on the subject of “liberalism and empire” and (he argues) the dependence of the former on the latter. The essay as a whole is an extended discussion of our current end-of-history era, engaged with some of the same questions as Mark Lilla, Steven Pinker, and other writers frequently discussed in this space. But its conclusion speaks directly to the moment’s foreign policy debates, offering critiques of both the anti-imperial left and the interventionist right, qualified sympathy for what McCarthy calls “anti-liberal anti-imperialists” (like his magazine’s founder, Pat Buchanan, and the late George Kennan, who are “among our greatest critics” but “preach what a liberal nation will not hear”), before coming around to a qualified endorsement of a “conservative realism” in the service of a liberal empire:

docs.abstract: A response to the conservative case for immigration inaction.
docs.snippet: A response to the conservative case for immigration inaction.
docs.lead_paragraph: I haven’t commented on the border situation since my column a few weeks ago, mostly because it’s the kind of situation (there are so many these days) where it’s easier to say what should have been done in the past than to figure out what the correct policy course is right now. But as House Republicans debate what kind of legislative response they intend to support, I want to say something briefly about the argument that they shouldn’t back any response at all, on the theory that since the president has already claimed sweeping, dubiously-legal powers over spending flows and immigration enforcement, fixing the mess should be his responsibility alone.

headline.main: Should Republicans Do Anything About the Border Crisis?

docs.abstract: In 1962, President Kennedy offered a primer in how to prevent an episode involving an airplane from escalating into conflagration.
docs.snippet: In 1962, President Kennedy offered a primer in how to prevent an episode involving an airplane from escalating into conflagration.
docs.lead_paragraph: On Oct. 27, 1962, at the zenith of the Cuban missile crisis, President Kennedy learned that an American U-2 spy plane had unintentionally penetrated Soviet air space near Alaska, drawing a complaint from the Soviets. He was concerned that the Soviet leader, Nikita Khrushchev, or those around him, might view the incursion as the deliberate forerunner of a full-scale United States invasion of his territory, which could lead quickly to nuclear war. He persuaded them that it was an accident. Of the American pilot, Kennedy bitterly said, “There is always some son of a bitch who doesn’t get the word.”

headline.main: Malaysia Airlines Flight: History's Lessons in Crisis Management

docs.lead_paragraph: Poetry may be a noble vocation, but poets are generally an impecunious lot. Resigned to significantly less than blockbuster sales and often saddled with student loans, they’re on intimate terms with arrears. A handful of them will gather Friday night at Berl’s Brooklyn Poetry Shop for “Write Off Debt,” a reading that revolves around the concept. Organized by Ashleigh Lambert and featuring her fellow poets Max Cohen, Dustin Luke Nelson, Allyson Paty, Niina Pollari, Christopher Salerno and Emily Toder, the evening aims to imagine fresh approaches to debt.

Another victim, naked except for a black bra, lay on the field, her gray hair mixing with the green grass, one leg broken and her body torn.

docs.lead_paragraph: Kill or be killed isn’t the official tag line of “The Purge: Anarchy,” but it fits. It would also make a more suitable title for this satisfyingly creepy, blunt, down-and-dirty thriller, one of those follow-ups that improves on the original. Once again, it’s a new morning in future America, and crime is still down, as is unemployment. The only thing that appears to be keeping the peace and assuring prosperity is the government-sanctioned annual bloodletting, that one night a year in which the citizenry can run amok without punishment. The word anarchy is purely superfluous.

docs.lead_paragraph: For more than 30 years, Bill Porter has been one of the most prolific translators of Chinese texts, while also developing into a travel writer with a cult following. Under the pen name Red Pine, the 70-year-old resident of Port Townsend, Wash., has translated over a dozen books of poetry and religious texts, including collections of poems by Hanshan and Song Boren, the Daoist classic Dao De Jing and numerous Buddhist sutras. Under his own name, he has also published travel works like “Zen Baggage: A Pilgrimage to China” and “Road to Heaven: Encounters With Chinese Hermits.”

docs.lead_paragraph: On most days of the two-week International Keyboard Institute and Festival, a popular annual venture sponsored by Mannes College the New School for Music, there are two piano recitals each evening. So it was on Wednesday, the third full day of the festival. For the early-evening Prestige series, which mostly presents exceptional younger artists, the award-winning 32-year-old German pianist Alexander Schimpf played a varied program culminating with Beethoven’s mighty “Hammerklavier” Sonata. Later that evening, the Israeli pianist Alon Goldstein, admired for the refinement and imaginativeness of his performances, played a formidable program on the Masters series. The recitals were presented at the intimate concert hall of the Mannes College building on the Upper West Side, which seats just 275.

docs.abstract: John le Carré recalls Philip Seymour Hoffman’s intensity in performing the role of a self-destructive German intelligence officer in the film adaptation of his novel “A Most Wanted Man.”
docs.snippet: John le Carré recalls Philip Seymour Hoffman’s intensity in performing the role of a self-destructive German intelligence officer in the film adaptation of his novel “A Most Wanted Man.”
docs.lead_paragraph: I reckon I spent five hours at most in Philip Seymour Hoffman’s close company, six at a pinch. Otherwise it was standing around with other people on the set of “A Most Wanted Man,” watching him on the monitor and afterward telling him he was great, or deciding better to keep your thoughts to yourself. I didn’t even do a lot of that: a couple of visits to the set, one silly walk-on part that required me to grow a disgusting beard, took all day and delivered a smudgy picture of somebody I was grateful not to recognize. There’s probably nobody more redundant in the film world than a writer of origin hanging around the set of his movie, as I’ve learned to my cost. Alec Guinness actually did me the favor of having me shown off the set of the BBC’s TV adaptation of “Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.” All I was wanting to do was radiate my admiration, but Alec said my glare was too intense.

(Showtime) LEE DANIELS’ THE BUTLER (2013) Inspired by the real story of Eugene Allen, Mr. Daniels follows a White House butler, Cecil Gaines (Forest Whitaker, above), and his wife, Gloria (Oprah Winfrey), as history — particularly the civil rights movement — unfolds over seven presidential administrations in what A. O. Scott, writing in The New York Times, called “a brilliantly truthful movie on a subject that is usually shrouded in wishful thinking, mythmongering and outright denial.” Robin Williams portrays Dwight D. Eisenhower; Liev Schreiber is Lyndon B. Johnson; and Alan Rickman is Ronald Reagan, with Jane Fonda as his wife, Nancy; Cuba Gooding Jr. and Lenny Kravitz are the fellow butlers who become Cecil’s close friends; and David Oyelowo is the older son whose politics Cecil eschews. “In part, their story is a chronicle of the generational misunderstanding that has occurred in upwardly mobile families of every background, especially in the baby boom era, when educated and restless young people turned against the parents who had sacrificed so much on their behalf,” Mr. Scott wrote. “ ‘The Butler’ has the historical insight and the generosity of spirit to honor the father and the son equally, and to look with skepticism at each’s point of view.” He added: “We remember those who marched and who stood up for themselves in the face of injustice. It is good to remember that, to paraphrase Milton, they also stand who only wait and serve.”

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Poland and Britain expressed doubt in Hitler’s willingness to keep the peace in 1939.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Poland and Britain expressed doubt in Hitler’s willingness to keep the peace in 1939.
docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — There were ample indications today [July 18] that both British and Polish official quarters continue to be highly skeptical of Berlin reports that Adolf Hitler is now prepared to seek a peaceful solution of the Danzig issue on the basis of terms which could be considered by Warsaw. Almost as if these reports had not been broadcast Poland issued today a new warning to the Fuehrer. A semiofficial communiqué issued in Warsaw read: ‘‘Quite apart from the manner in which Germany may desire to incorporate Danzig in the Reich, Polish political quarters declare that the very fact of such an incorporation would constitute an inadmissible violation of the present political and juridical state of affairs and would evoke the appropriate response.’’ This response, if previous Polish declarations are to be trusted, would be in the form of the use of force by Warsaw to restore the status quo ante in the Free City. In a declaration in the House of Commons at the beginning of last week Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain made it clear that should Warsaw determine to resist an attempted change from within or without in the status of Danzig, Britain, backed by France, would come to its aid. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 19, 1939

headline.main: 1939: London and Warsaw Skeptical

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Shooting at an integrated restaurant in Atlanta in 1964.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Shooting at an integrated restaurant in Atlanta in 1964.
docs.lead_paragraph: ATLANTA — Restaurant owner Redell Crosby last night shot and critically wounded a 22-year-old white man who entered his integrated restaurant with other whites shouting that Negroes should leave. The shooting coincided with racial outbursts in other Southern cities, including St. Augustine, Fla., and Philadelphia, Miss. Police said five white men who entered Mr. Crosby’s drive-in restaurant were arrested and charged with assault in a scuffle that preceded the shooting. The victim of the shooting was identified as Maurice Lawson of Atlanta. Mr. Crosby was arrested and charged with wounding Mr. Lawson. He was released on $1,500 bond. Detective Tony Quave said Mr. Lawson and the five told the Negroes in the restaurant, “You just have to go.” Mr. Quave said the white men attacked two of the Negroes, punching one in the nose, before Mr. Crosby pulled his pistol. Mr. Crosby held his fire and ordered the white men to leave. All left except Mr. Lawson, who advanced on the restaurant owner with a beer bottle. Mr. Crosby then began shooting. A few blocks from Mr. Crosby’s restaurant, a white man and his son were wounded by blasts from a shotgun fired by Negroes from a passing car. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 19, 1964

headline.main: 1964: Anti-Negro White Is Shot

docs.lead_paragraph: West Africa’s hub for nongovernmental organizations and international agencies, Dakar draws a cosmopolitan mix of travelers to its dusty downtown streets and surf-pounded coastline. It’s a city of hustlers and traders, bargainers and touts, eager to show you something or sell you something and not always dissuaded by a polite “non, merci.” Keep saying it. Daytime streets are crowded with men in sharp suits and women rustling in the hand-dyed polished cottons called bazins. At night, intimate restaurants offer Lebanese and French-influenced dishes or simple but fresh grilled fish with Creole sauce. Much later, the dance clubs in Plateau and Almadies, along with the calls to prayer, resound into the early morning.

Since so many of the criticisms of the reformist tendency have focused on issues where there either isn’t a definite “reform” position or where our ideas are more modest and incremental than the received wisdom about what American conservatism “must” do, I’m concerned that my responses — whether on immigration, foreign policy, the culture war, or climate change — have contributed to the sense that reform conservatism somehow has an ambition problem … that it’s a plausible first step toward a new right-of-center agenda, but lacks (or hasn’t yet been gutsy enough to advance) the Big Ideas that conservatism really needs to matter in American policy debates again. docs.lead_paragraph: At my high school, two students were expelled for getting into a fight wherein a teacher was injured. In addition, two students who filmed the fight — and later circulated the video among students — were also threatened with expulsion. Expelling students for filming fights is unheard-of in my district. The school said it had grounds to expel the two who took the video, as outlined by the handbook given to all students: “Students may be disciplined for any other misconduct which is deemed by school authorities to be disruptive or to interfere with the educational process.” There seems to be no rule, however, explicitly banning filming and circulating a fight. How much does students’ ignorance of a rule matter when determining a punishment? Is it ethical for a school to expel students for something they reasonably don’t know to be wrong? NAME WITHHELD, CLEVELAND

docs.abstract: “The Girls of August,” No. 13 on the hardcover fiction list, is the novelist Anne Rivers Siddons’s 13th best seller.
docs.snippet: “The Girls of August,” No. 13 on the hardcover fiction list, is the novelist Anne Rivers Siddons’s 13th best seller.
docs.lead_paragraph: Enemy Territory: The Southern novelist Anne Rivers Siddons is a fixture on the best-seller list — “The Girls of August,” new this week at No. 13, is her 13th book to land on the hardcover fiction list. So is 13 a lucky number for Siddons? Maybe not, judging from the largely disappointed comments readers are posting online about “The Girls of August.” But Siddons has overcome negative reviews before. As a student at Auburn University in the late 1950s, she was fired from the campus newspaper for defying the administration with a scorching column in support of integration (an incident that later found its way into her novel “Heartbreak Hotel”). “Never write a column when you’re mad or sick or disgusted, or all three,” she proclaimed early in the offending essay. “These are the things that make bad little columnists get reprimanding letters from the intelligentsia. Only the greenest, foolhardiest, most naïve amateur would broach a forbidden subject in Enemy Territory. . . . Meet an amateur par excellence.” Later in the same column she mulled the word “tolerance” — “It’s a grown-up word. Children and mobs do much better with four-letter ones” — and criticized people who were content to let their “moral petticoats” drag in the “good old Southern mud.” Auburn finally did integrate in 1964, seven years after that column, and the school eventually forgave Siddons for her justified dudgeon. It awarded her an honorary doctorate of humane letters in 1997, and organized a tribute to her last fall on the anniversary of the column’s publication date.

docs.abstract: David Grossman’s book in verse is an intimate study of grief and mourning.
docs.snippet: David Grossman’s book in verse is an intimate study of grief and mourning.
docs.lead_paragraph: The emblematic Man, any man, every man — dazed, heartsick, utterly bewildered — suddenly pushes away his dinner and gets up from the kitchen table. He can’t take it any longer — the overwhelming, claustrophobic grief, which has hollowed him out — and so he decides to go “there.” But where is there? That’s what the emblematic Woman, any woman, every woman, can’t figure out. That’s what she wants to know. She understands, this woman who is also a mother, a wife, that there is no place to go when you’ve lost a child. You are already wounded by disaster, forever bereft. “In an instant we were cast out / to a land of exile,” she remembers. But this man can’t sit still any longer. The trouble has taken him over again. And so he sets out to go “there” anyway. It has been five years, and he is determined to see his dead son one more time, though no one has ever made the journey and come back alive. Like a figure in a myth, he is going to walk across a divide, leaving the living behind, the innocent ones, who still exist inside of ordinary time.

docs.snippet: Patricia Lockwood’s second poetry collection continues her interrogation of gender, nature and sexuality.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s always wrong to judge a poem by its retweets, but when a literary work, by a poet not world famous for something else, gets hundreds of thousands of “shares,” “likes” and other such notices online, within weeks of publication, it’s time to ask why. That is what happened, in 2013, to Patricia Lockwood’s “Rape Joke.” Like rape itself, “Rape Joke” was no joke: “The rape joke is that you were 19 years old,” it began. “The rape joke is that he was your boyfriend. . . . The rape joke is that you had been drinking wine coolers. Wine coolers! Who drinks wine coolers? People who get raped, according to the rape joke.” To readers who had suffered similar outrages, Lockwood offered wit and a fed-up solidarity; to others, the poem brought news.

docs.lead_paragraph: Astra Taylor is a documentary filmmaker who has described her work as the “steamed broccoli” in our cultural diet. Her last film, “Examined Life,” depicted philosophers walking around and talking about their ideas. She’s the kind of creative person who was supposed to benefit when the Internet revolution collapsed old media hierarchies. But two decades since that revolution began, she’s not impressed: “We are at risk of starving in the midst of plenty,” Taylor writes. “Free culture, like cheap food, incurs hidden costs.” Instead of serving as the great equalizer, the web has created an abhorrent cultural feudalism. The creative masses connect, create and labor, while Google, Facebook and Amazon collect the cash.

docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a certain sense of fatedness that emerges in the 13 espionage novels Alan Furst has written about Europe before and during World War II, even if it’s never quite enunciated in their wry, reticent storytelling. It has to do with the nature of the genre. Furst’s makeshift spies act with courage, but their choices are shaded with a brutal irony, darkened by what we readers, a few paces further along in history, know will be coming for them and the people they care about: the battlefields, the camps. The consolation Furst offers for this knowledge is present in a careful hedonism, which insists on the heightened beauty of the evanescent during wartime — the unexpected pleasure of a meal or a glass of wine, a night in bed with a stranger as it snows outside, anything human.

docs.abstract: A boutique hotelier has turned this former gay landmark the San Vicente Inn into a chic, affordable hotel — and he’s not done yet. For now, summer looks good on the 29-room property with its cleaned-up grounds.
docs.snippet: A boutique hotelier has turned this former gay landmark the San Vicente Inn into a chic, affordable hotel — and he’s not done yet. For now, summer looks good on the 29-room property with its cleaned-up grounds.
docs.lead_paragraph: In West Hollywood, the San Vicente Inn is gradually being transformed by the boutique hotelier Jeff Klein, who is garnering lots of attention for turning the historically gay, seedy hotel into a clean and chic place for the young and beautiful to shack up on a budget (rooms range from $99 to $209 per night). Now known as the San Vicente Bungalows, the 29-room property has undergone basic renovations — like spiffed-up bathrooms, now stocked with Malin & Goetz products — that are attracting the 20- to 30-something international jet set. In addition to bright and cozy digs, guests enjoy free breakfast and can rent beach cruisers ($15 for 4 hours) to ride out to places like Venice Beach and Santa Monica, each just about 45 minutes away by bike. Even the locals are popping in for a swim — access to the pool and newly landscaped grounds is $35/day. Eventually, the now-charming place will get a complete makeover. So T checked into the buzzy little oasis to memorialize things as they stand now, while summer is in full swing.

headline.main: A Buzzy Hotel Oasis in West Hollywood

docs.lead_paragraph: Michael Sokolove’s cover story in this week’s magazine describes the downfall of Penn State’s former president, Graham Spanier. Gail Bichler, the magazine’s art director, said that because the article was about Spanier’s silence, she cropped Bryan Schutmaat’s portrait of him. ‘‘We thought focusing attention on his mouth was a powerful way to illustrate this,’’ she said. And Bichler said that showing him in casual dress (he also sat for photographs in a suit and tie) was a way to reflect the personal nature of Spanier’s discussions with Sokolove. The image was shot in color, but it was converted to black and white to give the cover a somber feel and make it more graphic.

headline.main: Under Cover: Silent Picture

Bush. “Yes, it is a probing and unsettling inquiry into the recent political and military history of the United States, but it is also a bracing and invigorating philosophical skirmish,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “The tension between those two registers — between hard facts about state violence and devilish abstractions about causes and consequences — is what gives the film some of its energy and suspense.” The film, he added, “is a cat-and-mouse game in which each player thinks he’s the cat, making it both thrilling and disconcerting to watch. docs.abstract: According to my mother’s prison records, she served around 17 weeks in “The Hole”—solitary confinement. Only for her it wasn’t so solitary. She had me.
docs.snippet: According to my mother’s prison records, she served around 17 weeks in “The Hole”—solitary confinement. Only for her it wasn’t so solitary. She had me.
docs.lead_paragraph: At a time when most infants rock in cradles, take naps on grandma’s shoulder or play bouncy-bounce on a knee, I crawled around in a 4-by-6-foot concrete box the size of a small closet. Instead of the background lullaby from a pull toy in a crib, I would have heard “Chow time!” yelled through the slot in the steel door and then a slam — the food port in our prison cell in solitary confinement. I was born in prison; I spent part of the first year of my life in “the hole.”

headline.main: Immaculate Incarceration: A Baby in Solitary Confinement

docs.lead_paragraph: LONDON — One of the most interesting and, perhaps, significant points in connection with the murder of Alice Mackenzie is one to which much attention has not yet been called. At the time of the August, September and November murders last year the number of constables on patrol duty in what is known as the ‘‘murder district,’’ covered by Commercial street and Leman street stations, was strengthened by 100 extra men from other divisions. There were at that time 300 men in uniform and plain clothes on night duty in this comparatively small area. As the excitement died away this extra force was gradually diminished.

headline.main: 1889: Jack The Ripper Said to Have Connection With Police

docs.abstract: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: Two people were shot in clashes between roving gangs and police in Harlem in 1964.
docs.snippet: Highlights from the International Herald Tribune archives: Two people were shot in clashes between roving gangs and police in Harlem in 1964.
docs.lead_paragraph: NEW YORK — For the third consecutive night police broke up an unruly, bottle-throwing crowd in the Negro community of Harlem tonight [July 20]. The steel-helmeted, nightstick-waving police scattered the two separate crowds without firing a pistol shot. Neither police nor members of the crowds were injured. Two Negroes were shot and wounded early today in clashes between roving gangs and scores of police. Bottles, rocks and Molotov cocktails rained down from tenement rooftops and smashed in the littered streets. In the weekend of riots, police said that one Negro was killed and 116 civilians and 18 policemen were injured. At least 45 stores were broken into and looted or damaged. The violence, and demands from civil-rights leaders that the city act to protect the Negroes, prompted the mayor’s office today to order a study of complaints of police brutality. Regular meetings between Harlem leaders and city officials were also arranged. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, July 21, 1964

headline.main: 1964: Harlem Riots Flare Anew; 2 Negroes Shot

docs.snippet: In “Lucky Us,” the novelist Amy Bloom describes the improvised passage through the 1940s by two half sisters, their father and loves.
docs.lead_paragraph: These two things about Amy Bloom’s surprise-filled “Lucky Us” are indisputable: It opens with a terrific hook and closes with an image of exquisite resolution. But that opening sets off a string of serial adventures, and it’s not until the book ends that all the pieces fall into place. Ms. Bloom does not write deep-dish, straightforward yarns for readers who enjoy conventional drama. She writes sharp, sparsely beautiful scenes that excitingly defy expectation, and part of the pleasure of reading her is simply keeping up with her. You won’t know where “Lucky Us” is headed until, suddenly, it’s there.

docs.abstract: A stage adaptation of James Dickey’s “Deliverance” will open the fall and winter season at 59E59 Theaters.
docs.snippet: A stage adaptation of James Dickey’s “Deliverance” will open the fall and winter season at 59E59 Theaters.
docs.lead_paragraph: A stage adaptation of James Dickey’s “Deliverance” will open the fall and winter season at 59E59 Theaters, that Off Broadway organization announced on Sunday. Based on the 1970 novel, which also inspired the 1972 movie of the same name starring Burt Reynolds, Jon Voight, Ned Beatty and Ronny Cox about an ill-fated canoe trip through the backwoods of Georgia, “Deliverance” is slated to have its world premiere on Oct. 10 as part of the Godlight Theater Company’s 20th anniversary celebration. Because of the more graphic scenes of the story, approving the theatrical version a “was quite a decision to make,” Peter Tear, 59E59’s executive producer, said by phone. He said that the playwright Sean Tyler, who adapted the story, had done “a tremendous job.” Other season highlights include “On a Stool at the End of the Bar ”(Nov. 14 through Dec. 14), Robert Callely’s work about a family’s reaction to a loved one’s long-held secret. Alex Webb’s “Cafe Society Swing: A True Story,” a musical revue based on the 1940s jazz venue that became New York City’s first racially integrated nightclub, will follow from Dec. 16 through Jan. 4. That will also represent the return of Evan Pappas (“Chorus Line,” “My Favorite Year,”) to New York stages for the first time since 2007, when he was badly injured in a car accident while touring with “On Golden Pond.” “Evan was one of those adored New York performers,” Mr. Tear said. “So people were terribly excited to hear he’s coming back.” Also slated for the season is the Crossroads Theater Company’s production of Walter Mosley’s “Lift” (Oct. 21 through Nov. 30); Little Opera Theater of New York’s performance of Carlisle Floyd’s “Slow Dusk” and “Markheim” (Dec. 5 through 14); and “Beware of Young Girls: Kate Dimbleby Sings the Dory Previn Story” (Dec. 16 through Jan. 4). More information is at 59e59.org.

headline.main: ‘Deliverance’ to Open 59E59’s New Season

docs.lead_paragraph: “The crisis of young migrants at the Texas border is a test of American values,” writes The New York Times editorial board, “One of those surprise exams that history now and then throws our way: Here are 57,000 helpless children. We are a nation of 300 million. Do we spit on them, or give them blankets and beds?” It’s a test the country may be flunking, according to the editorial. In neighboring Arizona, “Hearing that migrant children were being sent to the town of Oracle, a county sheriff instigated a protest that ensnared a busload of bewildered YMCA campers. A disbarred former county attorney running for governor has an ad showing a Mexican flag swallowing up a map of Arizona and the slogan ‘Before It’s Too Late.'” The crisis “emboldens demagogues in Washington” as well, the board writes. “Mr. Obama has the obligation to act the grown-up” when dealing with an obstructionist Congress, “but he can be a tepid ally where unauthorized immigrants are concerned, since he sees the issue through a calculating lens that overlooks the moral urgency to act.” And urgent the situation is.

headline.main: Morning Views

docs.lead_paragraph: Focaccia is a dimpled flatbread that can take a number of toppings, like a pizza but breadier. docs.abstract: This sauce is a tomato jam that tastes more like a richly spiced ketchup. A long simmer is important.
docs.snippet: This sauce is a tomato jam that tastes more like a richly spiced ketchup. A long simmer is important.
docs.lead_paragraph: This is inspired by a recipe for a delicious tomato jam in the chef Matthew Kenney’s cookbook, “Matthew Kenney’s Mediterranean Cooking.” My version is not as sweet as his; I decided to call it ketchup rather than jam because to me, it tastes like a richly spiced ketchup, with sweet and sour flavors and a little kick from the cayenne. A long simmer is important for cooking the sauce to the right consistency and for concentrating the flavors. After that, I put the ketchup through a food mill to achieve smoother texture, but that step is optional. I salt toward the end of cooking because the mix will reduce quite a lot and it’s too easy to oversalt if you salt before that happens. However, be sure to use enough salt to balance out the sweetness and bring out the spice.

headline.main: Spiced Tomato Ketchup

docs.abstract: Sweet, juicy heirloom tomatoes can be made into a concassé that works as well with vegetables as it does with pasta or grains.
docs.snippet: Sweet, juicy heirloom tomatoes can be made into a concassé that works as well with vegetables as it does with pasta or grains.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sometimes, I can’t bear to cook sweet heirloom tomatoes. I love this concassé with pasta or grains, but this time, I decided to use it as a sauce for Swiss chard. I steamed the chard to wilt it, heated it in a little bit of olive oil, then piled it on my plate and spooned the tomato sauce on top. It’s a great combo, and now I think I’ll use it as the vegetable and sauce element of a big bowl. A little feta sprinkled over the top would not be lost on this.

headline.main: Heirloom Tomato Concassé with Wilted Swiss Chard

docs.abstract: School administrators agree that students complained about new lunch standards when they were first implemented in the fall of 2012—but tell researchers that by spring, the complaints had largely subsided.
docs.snippet: School administrators agree that students complained about new lunch standards when they were first implemented in the fall of 2012—but tell researchers that by spring, the complaints had largely subsided.
docs.lead_paragraph: While many schools have been gradually improving the quality and nutrition of their lunches in the last few years, the updated standards released by the United States Department of Agriculture (as directed by the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010), which most schools put in effect over the 2012-13 school year, meant larger, faster changes to lunches nearly across the board. Higher-fat milk is gone; schools are required to serve a vegetable and a fruit daily; there can be no trans fat; and half of the grains offered must be whole grains (in the 2014-15 school year, all grains must be whole grains).

headline.main: Research Suggests Students Adjusting to New School Lunches

docs.lead_paragraph: More than 700 million women alive today were married as children, and about 250 million of them — more than one in three — were wed before they reached 15, Unicef said in a study released Monday, on the eve of an international meeting in London, the Girl Summit, sponsored by Unicef and the British government. It aims to mobilize efforts to end female genital mutilation and child, early and forced marriages. The study said child marriage remains widespread in parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. South Asia is home to almost half of all child brides worldwide, the study found. While an adolescent girl today is about a third less likely to be subjected to genital mutilation compared with 30 years ago because of activism, legislation and changing attitudes, Unicef said that in countries where it is still practiced, parents “continue to compel their daughters to undergo the procedure because of strong social pressure.”

headline.main: Study Tracks Millions of Child Brides

docs.lead_paragraph: Much about the current Bolshoi Ballet season at the Lincoln Center Festival is unexplained. Since other Western cities have seen this Moscow company’s productions of “Coppélia,” “Lost Illusions,” “Jewels,” why isn’t New York seeing them? All of them would expand our idea of the troupe. And why has the company not brought Evgenia Obraztsova, Ruslan Skvortsov or Vyacheslav Lopatin? Each has made a striking impression in one or more leading roles in recent live broadcasts by the company; Ms. Obraztsova, in particular, is one of the world’s most exquisite classical stylists. You’d think that a troupe that lost Natalia Osipova and Ivan Vasiliev in 2011 would be working harder to prove that it has an abundance of remaining stars.

docs.snippet: Scientists said that record-setting rains in the weeks before the landslide that killed 43 people in March in Oso, Wash., had clearly played a role, and, possibly, logging.

docs.snippet: Dozens of Turkish police officers were detained on Tuesday and accused of spying on Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his top aides.
docs.lead_paragraph: Dozens of Turkish police officers were detained on Tuesday and accused of spying on Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his top aides, news agencies reported. The Istanbul chief prosecutor’s office, in a statement carried by the semiofficial Anadolu News Agency, said the officers had fabricated an investigation into a supposed terrorist group as a pretense to spy on top officials. More than 500 prominent figures have been illegally wiretapped since 2010, CNN Turk television reported, citing the prosecutors’ office. More than 100 officers have been charged with falsifying evidence, illegal wiretapping and espionage, and 67 were taken into custody in a 22-city security operation. Some of those who were detained were involved in a corruption inquiry that ensnared Mr. Erdogan’s close circle and forced four ministers to resign in December, news reports said. Mr. Erdogan has said the graft investigation was driven by people loyal to Fetullah Gulen, a cleric who lives in Pennsylvania and is a former ally who still has influence in various state institutions. Sinan Ulgen, a visiting scholar at Carnegie Europe in Brussels, called the arrests “the latest episode in the war waged against the Gulen community.”

headline.main: Turkey: Officers Arrested in Spy Case

docs.abstract: The United Nations expressed concern about the possible spread of polio in the war-ravaged countries of Syria and Iraq and beyond on Tuesday.
docs.snippet: The United Nations expressed concern about the possible spread of polio in the war-ravaged countries of Syria and Iraq and beyond on Tuesday.
docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations expressed concern about the possible spread of polio in the war-ravaged countries of Syria and Iraq and beyond on Tuesday despite the biggest vaccination campaign undertaken in the history of the Middle East. A report by the World Health Organization and Unicef said that 36 children had been paralyzed by the polio virus in Syria since the disease first reappeared there last October after a 14-year absence. Polio also has been detected in two Iraqi children in Baghdad, and it paralyzed one of them in April, the report said. Although 25 million children under the age of 5 have been vaccinated multiple times in seven Middle East countries under an emergency campaign, the report said many Syrian children missed out because of fighting and restrictions on distributing medical aid. The report said 765,000 Syrian children under 5 live in hard-to-reach areas. Polio, which is spread by feces, was thought to be nearly eradicated a few years ago, but it has spread in some fragile countries this year. In May, the W.H.O. declared a global health emergency because of the resurgence, imposing travel restrictions on Pakistan, Syria and Cameroon because the virus had spread from those countries to neighbors.

headline.main: U.N. Warns of Polio Risk in War Zones

docs.lead_paragraph: “As much as I love living in New York, nothing’s better than being by the sea,” Lisa Marie Fernandez says. For the designer and stylist, known for her sculptural bikinis and chic après-beach layers, spending time in exotic maritime locales is not only relaxing, but also a job requirement of sorts. “I love to explore and get inspiration, but also, I like to live and breathe this lifestyle,” she says. “I love holiday clothing — bohemian caftans and sandals and barefoot and bathing suits. I’m really that person.” This month, on the tail end of a summer European trip that included stops in Paris and Capri, Fernandez traveled for the first time to the mountainous Mediterranean island of Corsica. What was originally planned as a weeklong jaunt stretched out to nearly twice that amount when Fernandez found out that her friend Laure Heriard Dubrueil, the owner of Miami’s the Webster boutique whose family has a house on the island, was heading over. “It’s really incredible that you can go to a place so close to France that’s so wild and refined and understated and not polluted with too much of anything,” Fernandez says. Here, she shares snaps and tales from the trip with T.

headline.main: Lisa Marie Fernandez’s Beachy Corsican Getaway

docs.snippet: Exploring the Bonavista Peninsula, one of Newfoundland's most dramatic appendages, two decades after a fishing moratorium was declared.
docs.lead_paragraph: Bruce Miller throttled back the engines of his 27-foot boat and entered the pinched harbor at Ireland’s Eye, an uninhabited, rock-rimmed island that lies eight miles off another, much larger island: Newfoundland. Scattered piles of weathered, gray boards dotted the steep, grassy banks like forgotten kindling. The captain held up a black-and-white 8-by-10 photo that echoed the view circa 1940. Back then, the timber stacks were clearly houses, schooners rested at anchor, and on the farthest hill stood a white church. Now, in the church’s place, a steeple lay in the tall grass. Worshipers last attended a service here in 1965, before a government resettlement policy forcibly moved the 157 residents of the remote fishing village, or “outport,” to larger communities in order to centralize the population.
